subtopic: PRESS REPORTS AS TO SUSPENSION OF IMPORTS TO BRITAIN FROM CANADA
speechtext:
A few days ago the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) asked me a question regarding the reported cancellation of Canadian newsprint contracts by the United Kingdom authorities. I stated at the time that I would have the matter looked into, and I am now in a position to make this brief statement.
As a result of various representations which have been made through both government and industry channels, the United Kingdom authorities have agreed to accept a definite tonnage of Canadian newsprint during 1946. The tonnage specified is considerably less than the original contract amount, but is nevertheless a not inconsiderable volume. Delivery of the remainder of the contract amount is postponed. The settlement which has been arrived at is, under all the circumstances, a reasonable one, and is I believe .acceptable to the Canadian producers.

"Have gone into this matter pretty thoroughly and any men with six figure numbers (above
Canadian Army-"Maple Leaf

600,000 at any rate) are definitely NRMA men. When they go active, and they could do so until after VE-Day, their number was changed as is the case with Usher.
"Something which bears an investigation and a good answer is how these men got posted to a First Division unit for return to Canada when they hadn't even left the U.K. on VE-Day. If this practice is being carried out by the reinforcement depots, which everything would lead me to suspect, then it's not good enough. There are a lot of fellows in L of C with high points who rate ahead of the NRMA men, of this category at least, who could be posted to units for return to Canada-not even taking into consideration the high point men from other active units who might like to have a look at Canada."
For Fighting Men
The Maple Leaf was established in Naples, in Italy, back in January, 1944, for Canadian Forces IN ACTION. The Maple Leaf has been produced for the soldiers, the fighting pien. The Maple Leaf has always done everything in its power to help the fighting men get a break. It's not stopping now.
This sort of business isn't funny. The men who volunteered to come overseas, who either went into action as volunteers or did their best as volunteers to see that the fighting men were equipped with the necessaries, deserve better treatment. This is an appeal on behalf of the volunteers who made this Canadian Army an army of which to be proud. All that is wanted is justice.	J.D.M.
(Editorial of September 20)
To Continue . . .
Men in garrison battalions, called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act, still non-active, but going home. The more we think about it, the less we like it. We like it even less than we did yesterday which was something considerably short of small huzza.
Let's get the picture straight:
These men were called up as far back as 1942. So they didn't go active. So maybe that's their business. Some blame the system, some the men. Some don't blame anybody. Some, on the other hand, think everything worked out just dandy. Some, on the other hand, wrist and elbow, still think Canadian men should never have gone overseas at all. It's a matter of opinion.
But, whatever the opinion, these men didn't come overseas until early in 1945. And they didn't come to Europe until after V-E day, after the shooting had stopped. And they came in garrison battalions. Those garrison battalions, if memory serves correctly, were slated for the occupation force.
And what happens? Some of the men in them, who have just come overseas, who have never fired a round anywhere but on the ranges, are steered into a First Canadian Infantry Division unit draft for HOME!
It may be said that they were specialists, tradesmen. If they were, all the more reason for holding them in Europe and releasing active specialists and tradesmen in L of C and CAOF with the necessary point score. It may be said that they weren't specialists, that tbey were just a bunch of guys. If they were, guard duty for a while with the CAOF on them would look good.
[Mr. Abbott. 1
It may be said that they were needed to fill up unit drafts. And it may be answered-has the need ever been THAT great? A good many gents with the points and shooting service would like to know.
It may be said that it's the "luck of the draw". And it may be answered that this is too serious a business to leave to chance, that there was no "luck of the draw" when men volunteered to come overseas and do something aDout a war that needed winning.
It may be said that it's the system, that's the way it's laid down, and that's the way it's got to be; that the men in charge of repat overseas are hamstrung, are doing their best in the face of policy. That is probably the real answer. But policy has been changed before and can be again.
This situation cannot be corrected too soon.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: I have a question to direct to the Minister of Labour. Has the government been informed of a threatened strike in the steel industry in sympathy with the automobile workers at Windsor, and if so, what steps are being taken to settle the dispute?

The answer to the first part of
the question of my hon. friend is, no; we have no information whatsoever of the kind which apparently he has received or obtained.
I should like to make a brief statement, if I may, in reply to the leader of the opposition. I believe he wanted to speak of the Ford dispute, not a steel dispute, and I assume that is the purport of the question.
Go ahead.

The hon. member for
Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) sent me notice of a question yesterday, but as we did not have orders of the day yesterday I was unable to reply to it. I think that I might now answer both questions at the same time.
The answer to the question of the hon. member for Cape Breton South is that the responsibility for bringing the strike of the Ford Motor company employees at Windsor to an end is one which must be assumed by the parties to the dispute. It is for the government to make available conciliation machinery by which assistance can be given to resolve such disputes. My department is ready at any moment to do so if the parties will take advantage of it. Up to the present moment it has not been possible to bring the parties into conference, but efforts in that direction are continuing.
It might be well if I were to give to the house the facts in connection with this strike. A board of conciliation had reported unanimously that the chief issue between the parties was the question of union security. The union demanded the application of the union shop principle as well as the check-off of

United Nations-Cultural Organization
union dues. Other questions such as increased wages, take-home pay, job security, et cetera, were brought before the board, but the board was unanimous in the view that such matters were required to be taken up with the regional war labour board for Ontario under the provisions of the wage control order. If, therefore, as some hon. members have suggested the Ford workers are on strike to obtain higher wages, and shorter hours of employment and similar improvements in conditions of employment, the way was open to them tc obtain consideration of such demands by the war labour boards under the wage control order. To the extent that they are on strike to obtain such demands, they are in violation of the provisions of the wage control orders.
However, be that as it may, the fact is that the Ford workers decided to strike, their objective being to force the Ford company to give them a contract which would be satisfactory, one which would include provision for the union shop and check-off. These were the issues which the board of conciliation said unanimously were "at the root of all the difficulties between the company and the union." The union concerned was not willing to wait to take their wage and other similar demands before the regional war labour board for Ontario, or to await the reply of the company to the recommendations made by the board of conciiation on the issues of union shop and check-off, but on the next day following consideration of that report called a strike of all the employees concerned. The union now is seeking further intervention by the government, and a demand has been made that the government take over the company's operations and appoint a controller.
The situation has been made more difficult by the fact that the picketing policy of the union has prevented officials and necessary office staff of the company from gaining access to their place of business, and by the withdrawal of the maintenance employees of the company-that is, the men engaged in the power houses. Such a policy makes conciliation practically impossible. I give these facts to the house because I feel that, both here and outside, attempts have been made to confuse the issue and to make it appear that there is a lack of effective government legislation to deal with the demands of the workers and to bring about a settlement of the dispute. This is wholly without foundation. There is no lack of effective legislation, and everything possible has been done by the Ontario Department of Labour and by the Dominion Department of Labour over the
past eighteen months to bring about a settlement of the dispute between the company and the union by conciliation.
May I close with this final word. I have this day wired the parties to the dispute, inviting them to attend a meeting in Toronto on Monday, October 15. I have also urged upon the union the desirability of giving company officials and necessary office employees access to their place of business prior to the meeting on Monday, which would remove an obstacle found by the company to attendance at a conference on a previous occasion, and I think would also create a condition which w'ould help make the conference a success. I have no advice as to whether or not the union will take this suggested action. It may mean that some hon. members will be asked for guidance by the union leaders, and if so I trust they will endorse my recommendation. At the proposed meeting would be representatives of the Dominion Department of Labour and also of the Ontario Department of Labour; arrangements already have been made to this effect.

subtopic: DISPOSAL OF PLANTS AND EQUIPMENT USED IN MAKING EXPLOSIVES AND FILLING SHELLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, because there has been criticism in respect of the destruction of war materials, I should like to make a statement in the hope of forestalling further criticism along the same lines.
As many hon. members are aware, following the first great war a number of accidents, some of which were fatal, resulted from the careless disposal of plants and equipment used for making explosives and filling shells. We are determined that no such unfortunate occurrence shall result from our disposal of the explosives and shell filling plants this time. For this reason, decontamination work is proceeding in all such plants prior to their being turned over to War Assets Corporation. This work is going forward under a decontamination committee of the Department of Munitions and Supply. This committee comprises a group of explosives experts. Their task is to ensure that, to the greatest extent possible consistent with safety, all machinery, equipment, buildings, and lumber shall be salvaged, and at the same time to ensure that no hazards remain.
No property is being destroyed without the express permission of this committee, and all salvageable materials after being thoroughly desensitized and freed of hazards will be turned over to War Assets Corporation for disposal.
So that hon. members may be made aware of the careful work being done by the decontamination committee and those under its control, and so that they may be assured that no salvageable material is being destroyed, I have asked the committee to arrange that newspaper men be permitted to visit a typical plant where they will see the decontamination methods being employed and vieiw the material being salvaged. They also will witness the destruction of a building which became so impregnated with dangerous explosives that no amount of decontamination could make it safe. This press party will visit the Bouchard 47696-59
works near Ste. Therese, Quebec, on Friday afternoon, October 12. I would welcome any hon. members, or any members of provincial legislatures, who might wish to accompany the party. The group will leave the Munitions and Supply office at 1155 Bishop Street, Montreal, in a chartered bus at 12.45 p.m., and will be returned to Montreal in the same bus.
At later dates, similar tours of the plants at Pickering, Ontario, and at Winnipeg, will be arranged, and should any hon. member of this house or of a provincial legislature wish to attend, he will be made welcome.

Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved the second reading of bill No. 14, for carrying into effect the agreement for a food and agricultural organization of the united nations between Canada and certain other nations and authorities.
He said: Mr. Speaker, a few days ago the house was kind enough to agree that full discussion of this measure should come on the motion for second reading, rather than upon the resolution presented at that time. I said to the house on that occasion that I would give a review of the circumstances leading up to the presentation of the bill to the house, and that I would be prepared to listen to any discussion in which hon. members might wish to take part with regard to the measure itself or other matters pertaining to it.
Item No. 9 on today's order paper is one calling for the second reading of bill No. 14, an act for carrying into effect the agreement for a food and agricultural organization of the united nations between Canada and certain other nations and authorities. At this time I am moving second reading of the bill which I have before me and which, I believe, is in the hands of all hon. members.
The explanatory note to the bill sets out the real reason for its being brought to the house, it states:
The purpose of this bill is to enable the government of Canada to give effect to the agreement for a food and agriculture organization of the united nations which is to be signed and come into force when twenty nations have notified their acceptance of the constitution set out in the schedule to the bill. The method proposed is to empower the governor in council to do whatever may be proper and expedient for carrying out the provisions of the constitution, or any recommendations of the conference of the organization, or its committees, made pursuant to such provisions. It is also provided that all expenditures incurred in carrying out the agreement shall be defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament.
I do not think I need go into detail to emphasize the importance of the measure now before us, but perhaps it would be proper
[Mr. Fraser.}
to give a historical review of the circumstances leading up to its introduction.
In the spring of 1943 a conference was called at Hot Springs, Virginia, by the then President of the United States, the late President Roosevelt. That meeting was attended by representatives of forty-four united nations. It was the first international conference to deal with post-war plans and development, and it seems fitting that the first conference held to carry into effect some of the principles set out in the Atlantic charter should be one having to do with food. Since agriculture is particularly related to the production of food products both in this countiy and elsewhere, this measure has been placed on the order paper under my name.
It has been shown that there is a need for improved nutritional conditions throughout the world. The benefits to be derived from improved nutrition in human welfare and international relations and in the interests of agriculture and other natural products industries is well recognized by all members of this house. The recommendations of the conference were to the effect that a permanent food and agriculture organization be established, and that in the meantime an interim commission be appointed to base upon the recommendations of the conference a constitution which could be submitted to the governments of the united nations, the adoption of which would result in the formation of a permanent organization. The chairman of that interim organization was Hon. L. B. Pearson. I think we in the Dominion of Canada have reason to be proud of the fact that Canada's representative was chosen as the first chairman of that organization.
Under the terms of the proposed constitution a maximum of twenty nations must become members before the organization can be formed. I have before me at this moment a list of the names of the nations which have signified their intention of becoming members. This list is composed of thirty names which I think should be placed upon Hansard. The following is the list of countries that have indicated their intention to accept the constitution of F.A.O.:
Australia
Belgium
China
Czechoslovakia
Denmark
Dominican Republic
Ecuador
Egypt
France
Greece
Guatemala
Haiti
Honduras
Iceland
India
Iraq
Liberia
Luxembourg
Mexico
Netherlands
New Zealand
Nicaragua
Norway

Philippines
Poland
Union of South Africa
United Kingdom United States Venezuela

United Nations Food Agreement
The organization will be an inter-governmental body. It will administer its own activities within the provisions of the constitution which are outlined in the schedule to this bill. There will be a director general appointed at the conference of the organization. An executive committee consisting of not less than nine and not more than fifteen members will be appointed by the conference and to which the conference may delegate powers. It will concern itself with studies of production and marketing problems as they relate to food, agriculture, forestry and fisheries, and it will endeavour to promote research work having to do with the solution of these problems. It will endeavour to render assistance to any government requesting such assistance. It will assemble and distribute official data and promote the development of information that can be coordinated internationally. It will serve the interests of both producers and consumers and function as an organization representing food, agriculture, fisheries and forestry in international deliberations with other international organizations of the united nations.
One matter that will be of interest to hon. members who are being asked to consent to this bill which will permit our taking part in the organization of this conference is the question of expense. I should like to set out the position in relation to the expenses of the organization. For the first year, when the organization is getting under way and when it will have only a small staff, F.A.O. will operate on a budget of $2,500,000. Any unspent balance will form a nucleus of a capital fund. The commission recommends that the average expenditures for the first five years should be estimated at about $5,000,000 yearly. A temporary apportionment of expenses has been recommended by the commission, and a division of the expenses among the different nations involved will be found at the end of the schedule to the bill which is before the house. No member nation will be asked to pay more than 25 per cent. The four major powers will assume 54-5 per cent of the total expenses. For the first year the United States will pay 25 per cent of the expenses, the United Kingdom 15 per cent, the Soviet Union 8 per cent, China 6-5 per cent and France 5-69 per cent. Canada is sixth in the list with 5-06 per cent. Provision is made for new members to the extent of two per cent of the total expenses. The contributions of liberated countries has been scaled down as a measure of temporary financial relief, but when world conditions 47696-59J
improve and they are able to pay more, the proportions allotted to some of the other countries will be reduced accordingly.
Those are the important facts in connection with the measure itself. The need for this measure being passed with as great dispatch as possible arises from the fact that the first meeting of the conference is to be held in Quebec, opening on Tuesday October 16. I assume that the nations that are mentioned as having already indicated their desire to be parties to the conference will be represented. We are sending a delegation representative of the government. A list of those who are to go will be available to members of the house as soon as the order in council appointing them is made complete. I should like to say to hon. members that those representatives will be largely officials of the departments of agriculture, fisheries and forestry under the Department of Mines and Resources and persons representing the health department or having to do with nutrition. The delegation will be made up largely of officials of the government taken from these different departments.
There will also be present as a representative of that organization the president of the farm federation, Mr. Hannam, as well as others who have been selected here and there to a limited extent. There are others who have been selected as delegates or as advisers to those who are delegates to the conference. This list will be made available at the earliest moment. As soon as it is placed before me it will be laid on the table so that it may be available to hon. members.
In addition to the officials of the departments, Hon. L. B. Pearson will be a delegate. I understand that the acting Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) will be there on Tuesday to open the meeting, and I have been asked to attend as a member of the government and as one of the delegates. My deputy will be a deputy representative of the government at that first meeting.
It is our desire to have this legislation passed in order that our membership in the conference may be made official along with others who will be gathered there and who have already taken suitable action in their own countries to make their position legal and official, and in order that we may be on the same footing as other delegations.
I would therefore move that the bill be given its second reading.
United Nations Food Agreement

I wonder if the minister would answer one question before he sits down. The explanatory note to the bill contains this statement:
. . . the agreement for a food and agriculture organization of the united nations which is to be signed . . .
The second paragraph of the preamble contains these words:
And whereas Canada is transmitting an instrument of acceptance of the constitution to the interim commission . . .
There is a little confusion as to whether the government has transmitted that instrument of acceptance to the interim commission or whether that is to be done after this measure is passed.
I understand that it has been prepared and will be forwarded as soon as the legislation is passed.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house has listened with interest to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) as he outlined the circumstances leading up to this proposal and gave a brief outline of the clauses of the bill. I am rising at this time to do two things: first, to commend the objective and the purpose of the measure, and second, to criticize the means by which the government is planning to set up and carry on this organization.
The bill provides for two things which were outlined by the minister: the carrying into effect of a certain agreement with respect to the food and agriculture organization of the united nations; and that all expenses in connection therewith shall be defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament.
As I said, we on this side approve the objective of the bill, but we criticize the manner in which it is proposed to administer it. The first question which we have to try to understand is, what is the agreement? There was an agreement made at the Hot Springs conference, which is referred to in the report of the interim commission, but I gather-and I presume it is a fair interpretation-that the government means by the agreement the terms of the constitution set out in the schedule of the bill.
Arising out of the Hot Springs conference there was an agreement that steps should be taken to form a united nations organization to try to improve the standards of nutrition and the standards of living of all peoples, and an interim commission was appointed to prepare complete plans for a permanent organization for that purpose. The report of that interim commission was tabled in this house in the early days of the session. It set out the form of constitution, and that form of

constitution is now included as a schedule to this bill. I asked the Minister of Agriculture a moment ago what the government has done by way of advising with respect to the government's acceptance of the agreement, and the minister said that they have the acceptance ready to go and are awaiting the approval by parliament of this measure before the advice goes forward.
In this bill, as I read it, the government is asking that power be given to the governor in council to do all "such things as appear to him to be necessary for carrying out the provisions of the constitution." The governor in council is to be given power by this bill to "make such appointments, establish such offices, make such orders in council and do such things as appear to him to be necessary" to carry this agreement into effect or to carry out the constitution as outlined in the schedule to the bill; and further, to carry out recommendations of the organization, which may comprise forty-five or more nations in which Canada has only one vote; and power also to carry out the recommendations of any committees that the organization may set up. These are very wide powers which the government seeks in connection with this bill. Three questions arise which every member of this house, I am sure, will want to think about. First, what are the essential features of this agreement or of this constitution or of this bill? Secondly, what recommendations may come forward from the conference which it aids in setting up, and what recommendations may come forward from the committees that the conference may set up? The bill aims to give the government power to carry out not only the recommendations of the conference of the organization, but the recommendations of committees of the conference. As the bill now7 stands, it is giving the government power to do all these things.
Let me refer for a moment to one or two of the essential features of the bill. The schedule contains twenty-six articles, and I want to refer to two or three of them. First of all article XVIII, from which I quote:
Upon approval of a budget the total amount approved shall be allocated among the member nations in proportions determined, from time to time, by the conference. Each member nation undertakes, subject to the requirements of its constitutional procedure, to contribute to the organization promptly its share of the expenses so determined.
As the minister has pointed out, the budget proposed for the first year is two and a half million dollars, of which Canada is expected to contribute 5 "06 per cent, or something over $125,000 the first year. In another place, not

United Nations Food Agreement
in the bill but in the report of the interim commission, as the minister pointed out, this organization expects that the expenses will be $5,000,000 a year after the first year. If the percentage allocated to Canada remains the same, 5-06 per cent, our contribution will come to more than $250,000 a year. The conference is given power to alter by a two-thirds vote the percentage that each nation will pay, but in any event the government of Canada will be committed on the passage of this bill to that figure for five years. In other words when we pass this bill we are committing ourselves to an expenditure of something over one million dollars-5-06 per cent of $2,500,000 the first year and 5-06 per cent of $5,000,000 for each of four years-and we cannot get out of it until the end of five years. It is clear that we are asked to commit ourselves to that expenditure for five years. At the moment I am not criticizing that feature of the measure; I am just pointing out what it is that we are being asked to do under this bill.
I have said that by the passage of this bill the government will be in a position to carry out the recommendations of the conference of from forty to fifty nations which this bill makes possible, and will be empowered to carry out also the recommendations of the committees of that conference. I think, therefore, that we should inquire as to what powers the organization is being given under this bill. Something of that may be seen in the preamble to the bill and in the outline of the functions of the organization given on page 3 of the schedule. The preamble states:
The nations accepting this constitution, being determined to promote the common welfare by furthering separate and collective action on their part for the purposes of:
raising levels of nutrition and standards of living of the peoples under their respective jurisdictions,
securing improvements in the efficiency of the production and distribution of all food and agricultural products,
bettering the condition of rural populations, and thus contributing toward an expanding world economy,
hereby establish the food and agriculture organization.
Then follows an outline of the functions of the food and agriculture organization once it is set up. Here is the outline in article I of the schedule:
1.	The organization shall collect, analyse, interpret, and disseminate information relating to nutrition, food and agriculture.
2.	The organization shall promote and, where appropriate, shall recommend national and international action with respect to:
(a) scientific, technological, social, and economic research relating to nutrition, food and agriculture;
(b)	the improvement of education and administration relating to nutrition, food and agriculture, and the spread of public knowledge of nutritional and agricultural science and practice;
(c)	the conservation of natural resources and the adoption of improved methods of agriculture production;
(d)	the improvement of the processing, marketing, and distribution of food and agricultural products;
(e)	the adoption of policies for the provision of adequate agricultural credit, national and international;
(f)	the adoption of international policies with respect to agricultural commodity arrangements.
There are even wider powers, because:
It shall also be the function of the organization:
(b) to organize, in cooperation with the governments concerned, such missions as may be needed to assist them to fulfil the obligations. . . .
And so on. I need not read it all. I have read sufficient to show, what the bill clearly indicates, that the purposes of the organization are very wide, as are the powers we are giving the government to carry out the recommendations of the organization.
I have outlined briefly the purposes of this permanent food and agriculture organization. I have shown something of their functions as set out in the bill and something of the powers being granted the government with respect to it, and I have said that we favour the objectives both of the conference and of this measure. I have said also that we object to the manner in which the government is proceeding to carry it out.
Three questions are raised in my mind, and, I am sure, will be raised in the minds of other members of the house: What is the need in Canada for this measure? What obligation does it place upon Canada, and what advantages will Canada derive from it?
With respect to the advantage to Canada, I do not think that anyone will question the advantage of trying to improve the nutritional standard of the Canadian people and of others. I have here a statement with respect to nutritional standards in Canada and in other countries, and I shall apply myself closely to it so that I can get through in two or three minutes.
With the coming of the new knowledge of nutrition we now know that inadequate diets, either in quantity or in quality, or in both, are responsible for much of present-day disease, sickness and lack of general good health. We now know also that even in such high standard of living countries as Canada and the United States, malnutrition and undernourishment are surprisingly widespread. Before the war the Canadian council of nutrition

United Nations Food Agreement
made a number of food surveys in the cities and rural areas. All these studies showed that a high percentage of the people were inadequately nourished. A shocking situation was revealed, for of the families not on relief, who were earning under $1,500 a year, 77 per cent had a diet too low in total calories; 80 per cent had diets deficient in calcium; 70 per cent had diets deficient in iron. The vitamin situation was then as bad; 61 per cent were deficient in vitamin A, 92 per cent were deficient in vitamin B and 60 per cent were deficient in vitamin C.
A former under-secretary of the United States department of agriculture stated that at least one-fourth of the people in that country who were not on relief had poor diets, and that three-fourths of the total population did not have fully satisfactory diets-and this in spite of the fact that that great nation is probably one of the best fed countries in the whole world.
With respect to Great Britain, the situation is not dissimilar. In 1939 a well known scientist, Sir Jdhn Orr, stated1 that the diet of at least fifty per cent of Britain's population fell short of a desirable standard of nutrition.
In Europe responsible authorities have drawn attention to the fact that prior to the war 80,000,000 people of the rural population of that continent were normally living on the verge of destitution, and that from 30 million to 40 million were permanently underfed. One of these authorities, Mr. F. L. McDougall, in 1935 said that if Europe were to raise its fluid milk consumption to a desirable standard it wrould be necessary to double the number of milch cows on the continent.
No statistical data are available to show the state of normal undernourishment and normal semi-starvation which is the every-day state of millions in Asia, but enough is known about periodic famines and the high death rates in such countries as India, China and Arabia to indicate that destitution and hunger to a degree are either always present or just around the corner for untold millions. So much for the need of an institution of this kind, not only for the benefit of our own country but for the benefit of other countries as well.
What obligations does this place upon Canada? First, by article XI, we are required to report to the organization the measures we take to try to carry out its purposes. Other countries are required to do the same. Then we are required to grant certain privileges and immunities to the organization -immunity from suit and exemptions from taxation. That will be found in article XV,
clause 2. We are required to pay at the moment 5-06 per cent of the cost, the total of which after the first year, it is estimated, will be around $5,000,000 a year, and we are required to do that for five years. After being in for four years we can give notice if we want to get out, but we have to pay for the fifth year before we can get out.
What are the advantages to Canada for that contribution of more than $1,000,000, and for other contributions by way of cooperation, which we shall make? We shall gain the experience of other countries through an international organization which one might call a little league of nations within the limited jurisdiction of food and agriculture. We shall no doubt receive some stimulus to the improvement of our standards of nutrition in this country. There will probably be some improvement in international understanding, probably some increase in the stability of our export trade and our domestic trade, and probably also some increased demand for our own products. As other nations begin to grow what we call protective foods, there will probably be demands for a greater amount of the agricultural products which we produce.
It may be asked, what means are to be employed by this international organization, in which we shall have only one vote and to which we shall contribute over a million dollars, to accomplish these ends? As I read the bill, it seems to me that the efforts are to be directed along three lines: research, the dissemination of already existing knowledge, and the exchange of services. I am sure that every hon. member will support the organization in such approaches to the objectives in this bill.
I believe that scientific research is the key which will unlock the door to greater production, greater consumption, and a higher standard of living among our people.
With respect to the dissemination of already known information, one of the lamentable facts in our society is that there is so much known information and so little of it which gets to the rank and file of our people. As one student has well put it, the accumulation of information far exceeds the assimilation of it by the people. To the extent, therefore, to which this organization succeeds in spreading already existing knowledge in Canada and outside of Canada, it will be doing good service.
The third means they propose to use to accomplish their ends is the exchange of services. In that way knowledge accumulated in one country, another country need not go to the expense of obtaining. There is an exchange of knowledge gained and duplication

United Nations Food Agreement
of effort is lessened. One of the great advantages to Canada of being a neighbour of the United States is that through the last two or three generations we have been able to draw upon the lessons they have learned from their researches and their experiments.
How does the organization propose to use these potential aids to progress? By applying them to five things. You see them in the outline of the functions of the organization: by raising the standards of nutrition, by increasing production, by increasing consumption, by improving distribution, and, in addition, in the conservation and development of our resources.
I cannot take time to-day-it is not necessary, before this house-to point out what great gains can be made in each of these directions. We know that the standard of nutrition can be raised, and as a preventive of illness and as a humanitarian objective it ought to be raised.
With respect to increasing production, one of the serious features of our economy in the past was the danger of surpluses; those who produced the world's food often produced a surplus, and they were frequently impoverished in the process. It is said that if every person in the world were adequately fed we would have to double our production. Well, if the nutrition of the world can be raised, let us hope that the threat of poverty to the people who in the past have raised the world's food will be banished. As our Social Credit friends to the far left here have often said in recent years, one of the weaknesses of our economy is the lack of purchasing power. With that I wholly agree. With the low wages we have had. with unemployment, with low prices for agricultural products, there has not been the purchasing power for farmers or for the workers who produced the things which farmers buy. So there has not been the necessary consumption of agricultural products. We have thus been able under that system to produce more than we could consume. Let us then bring all the research which can be brought to bear on solving the problem of increasing consumption, chiefly by increasing purchasing power.
Then comes the question of improving distribution. Reference is made to transportation, and the preservation of food by quick freezing and otherwise. Let me take a minute to tell the house of something I saw in France last January with respect to the effect of poor transportation on the nutrition and comfort of a country. They told us that four thousand of their bridges had been destroyed by bombing during the war, and that only some twelve hundred had been repaired. In France a good deal of transportation is by canals. They told
us that whereas they had had ten thousand ships carrying their goods, at that time only
4.500	were in operation, and only 900 available for interior transport. They told us that before the war they had 15,000 locomotives, and that after liberation there were only 1,200 fit to use, and even when we were there only
4.500	were in operation.
What was the result? In one part of France they had coal mines, and in Paris they were freezing because the allowance to each household was only a few pounds a week. In parts of France they grow sugar beets, but because these could not be hauled to sugar factories there was a shortage of sugar in Paris. In the outlying parts of France there were potatoes in large quantities, but in the absence of transportation facilities to move them there was a serious shortage in Paris.
These are typical of the kind of problem that this international organization is proposing to attack. It is the kind of thing we in Canada have been attacking alone, but now it is proposed that in cooperation with other countries, it shall be tackled jointly. What is Canada's answer to be to the Hot Springs conference? Personally I dislike the growth and expansion of bodies accountable to no responsible democratic assembly. They are apt to become little dictators within the jurisdiction given them. But to-day we are living in a world different from the world of a few years ago. We are living in a world which day by day is growing smaller, in which potential dangers increase daily, in which there are half a hundred nations separated by national boundaries, by national laws and by national traditions. In such a world Canada, like other nations, must make a choice. In such a world I think, and I am sure this house thinks, we must make some concession to internationalism. There must be some continuing approach to world understanding. There must be the maximum cultivation of good will. So we support the principle and the objective of this measure.
Under this proposal Canada will give directly more than a million dollars, and will make other contributions by way of cooperation with these other countries. Our return on this investment will be indirect, perhaps invisible; it may be that we will never be able to measure it. What the net result will be no man can tell. We could do a great deal with a million dollars toward improving the nutritional standards of the Canadian people, but as an investment in a healthier human race it is probable that we shall receive an even larger dividend. By this measure we are casting our bread upon the international waters, hoping it will return

manyfold. We do this as an investment in good will; we do it as an act of faith, hoping it will contribute to an expanding world economy, to a healthier human race, and to a more peaceful world.
From what I have said, Mr. Speaker, hon. members will gather that we are wholeheartedly in support of the purposes of this measure. I come now to the parts in connection with which I have some criticism to offer.
Portions of section 2 seem to have been copied verbatim from the statute ratifying certain treaties of peace in 1919, but that makes no difference to my criticism. In this measure we are giving too wide powers to the government, pow'ers wider than they need. The other measure referred to was an act to terminate a war. Whatver justification there may have been in 1919 does not exist now for surrendering the rights of parliament and giving the government a blank cheque to do as much or as little as it chooses in assisting in the setting up of this organization.
This bill should be meticulously examined in committee of the whole. Some of its clauses are objectionable for a number of reasons, some of which I shall mention. Section 2 of the bill provides that the governor in council may make such appointments as may be necessary. This is an intrusion upon the Civil Service Act. Surely the time has come when we should call a halt to making appointments outside that act. The government should discontinue the practice of seeking the power of appointment by the cabinet at the expense of the civil service commission. Too often in the past as new instruments of government have been created the power of appointment has been vested in the governor in council, which in fact means in the political minister, whoever he may be, in charge of the administration of the act. If the practice continues at the same rate as in the past, appointments under the Civil Service Act in accordance with the merit principle will become the exception rather than the rule.
Section 2 provides also that the governor in council may-
-establish such offices, make such orders in council and do such things as appear to him to be necessary for carrying out the provisions of the constitution.
That is, he may do what he considers necessary to carry out the recommendations of a body of forty-five nations, on which we are represented by only one vote, or for carrying out the recommendations of committees appointed by that organization. That is a most sweeping power to vest in a government. It is highly objectionable in principle; it is likely in practice to be a serious derogation
[Mr Bracken.]
from the legislative rights of parliament, and there is no restriction as to time. Sweeping powers of this kind may have some justification in war time, but they have none now, and they are not needed to carry out the constitution or the principles of this bill.
Section 2 also provides that the money shall be paid out of moneys provided by parliament. I believe that provision should be qualified by inserting after the words "provided by parliament" the words "for this purpose". Then each year we would know what votes, other than the amounts being now approved, were required by the government.
Section 3 requires a report of operations under the act to be laid before parliament "as soon as practicable after the close of each fiscal year". The phrase quoted is highly objectionable. It permits the Secretary of State for External Affairs to determine in his sole discretion when it is practicable to prepare and present this report. There is no limiting factor whatever. Other acts passed at the last session of parliament and in previous sessions indicate a more correct procedure in this respect. For example in the family allowance act, chapter 40 of the statutes of 1944, section 15 reads:
The minister shall submit to parliament within fifteen days of the commencement of the first session of parliament in each year a report of expenditures and administration in connection with this act during the previous fiscal year.
Likewise the Exports Credits Insurance Act, chapter 39 of the statutes of 1944, provides in section 26 as follows:
The Minister of Finance shall report to parliament on the operation of part 2 of this act within thirty days after the end of each fiscal year or, if parliament be not then sitting, within thirty days after the commencement of the next ensuing session thereof.
In the same way the Industrial Development Bank Act, which is chapter 44 of the statutes of last year, provides in section 29 that the president of the bank shall transmit to the Minister of Finance a full report within ten weeks after the end of each fiscal year. It is then provided that this report shall be laid before parliament within fourteen days if parliament is then sitting or, if parliament is not sitting, within fourteen days after the commencement of the next session. The appropriation act customarily has this clause:
A detailed account of the sums expended under the authority of this act shall be laid before the House of Commons of Canada during the first fifteen days of the then next session of parliament.

These sections indicate what is the correct procedure in a measure of this kind, and I would suggest that section 3 should be amended to provide something like the following:
The Secretary of State for External Affairs shall prepare and lay before parliament a report of operations under this act within thirty days after the end of each fiscal year or, if parliament be not then sitting, within thirty days after the commencement of the next ensuing session thereof.
My last point by way of criticism is this. The bill should contain a provision requiring all orders in council to be laid before parliament. That is not required in the present bill. I would suggest that a clause be inserted in the bill as follows:
A copy of all orders in council passed pursuant to this act shall be laid before parliament forthwith after the passage thereof if parliament be then sitting or, if parliament be in Teeess, then within fifteen days after the commencement of the next ensuing session.
We want to facilitate in every way the passing of this bill. We support whole-heartedly the objective of the measure. We do not think, however, that the government needs the wide powers contained in sections 2 and 3, and we respectfully suggest that the government consider some limitation upon those powers.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate on this very important measure I want my first words to be a tribute to the work of the representatives Canada sent to the Hot Springs conference, where this measure originated. The contribution of those who went there to represent Canada was outstanding; and in appreciation of their contribution the Hon. L. B. Pearson, our respresentative at Washington, was. made chairman of the interim committee which was given the job of drafting the present constitution. Mr. Pearson did a good job on that committee, and Canadians can be proud of some of our representatives abroad.
I believe there are few in the house who will make any objection to the purpose of the measure. So far as I can see, the objective is to bring into operation one of the freedoms set out in the Atlantic charter, 

freedom from want. There was a time in the world's history when it was thought that that could not be accomplished. Back in 1798 Robert Malthus, a prominent British economist, in an essay on food, propounded what has since been known throughout the world as the Malthusian theory, which stated, in effect, that we would always have want, and that the pressure of population against the available food supplies would always remain. To-day, however, a 47696-60
hundred and fifty years later, we realize that that theory is not sound, in at least so far as the western hemisphere is concerned. We have shown that through modern technical development and improvement in our agricultural methods and equipment, and through the greater use of fertilizers, we can secure freedom from want. The objective of the bill is to spread that freedom from want to other parts of the world, and surely there can be no objection to anything of that kind.
From a purely selfish point of view, Canada is keenly interested. We realize the significance of our interest when we remember that of the ten per cent of the world's food supplies exported, Canada supplies an amount entirely out of proportion to her population. If the measure will raise the nutritional standards of the- world, it will mean greater markets for Canadian food. The success of the legislation now before us to a great extent will depend upon the individual nations which have joined the conference, and upon whether they will be prepared to carry into effect some of the recommendations which undoubtedly will be made by the organization when it is established.
I cannot altogether agree with some of the deductions made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken). I find difficulty in reading into the bill anything in the nature of dictatorship, or anything which would suggest that the organization would have power to force its decisions upon members adhering to the constitution. As I read them, their powers are only by way of recommendations which they would make to the governments joining the organization.

Has the hon. member
read the provision respecting expenses?

Yes, I have read that provision, but I would point out that the amount of money we are being called upon to contribute is but a very small part of our budget. If we can raise the nutritional standards of the world and secure better markets for our agricultural products, I am convinced our bread cast upon the waters will return a hundredfold. In my view this is one of the best investments Canada could make, and I cannot see how we are committing ourselves to anything which in the future might cause us to regret our action. My one criticism would be that we have been late in taking action. As a matter of fact at the last session I suggested that we should then have ratified this constitution. Even from the purely selfish point of view, Canada should have been among the first instead of among the last of the united nations to effect ratification. If



United Nations Food Agreement
through this measure we can raise the nutritional standards of the world, we shall have accomplished something.
According to reports presented to the interim committee, if we are to have freedom from want, it would appear necessary to increase the food supplies of the world. I was surprised to read that, even to give a minimum nutritional standard to the peoples of the world, the total world's food production should be doubled. The suggestion is made that the production of cereals should be expanded 50 per cent, of meats 90 per cent, of milk and other dairy products 125 per cent, of vegetable oils 125 per cent and of fruits and vegetables 100 per cent. It will be necessary to produce more food per acre, and eventually to bring under cultivation every acre which can be developed economically, if we are to have freedom from want.
This organization has gathered statistics on nutrition, production and distribution, and is making them available to all nations so that they can increase not only their production but also their consumption of foods. I do not think any hon. member would object to that programme.
Some recommendations made to the interim committee I should have liked to see carried into the constitution. The original document drafted at Hot Springs made certain definite recommendations which it was expected the interim committee would draft into the constitution. One of the recommendations, having to do with the distribution of foodstuffs, was that cooperative organizations throughout the world should be used to a large degree in the process of distribution. Speaking of the cooperative movement, it is pointed out that the United States conference on food and agriculture has recommended the strengthening and expanding of the cooperative system in rural and urban areas. While I have not readily at hand the refer-5nce respecting cooperative organizations, I do know that their recommendations were definite, and that they emphasized that those organizations were taking an important part in the collection and distribution of foodstuffs.
We have large cooperatives in western Canada such as the wheat pools, and there are large consumer cooperatives in Great Britain handling the distribution of foodstuffs. They recommended that these organizations should be encouraged and given a greater place in the collection and distribution of food throughout the world. That recommendation has not been carried forward into the constitution, at least in any direct way. It

might be considered that it was implied, but I would have liked to see it in a more definite form.
Another thing to which I should like to direct the attention of the house is that as in the nineteen thirties, in certain sections of the world the production of food at the present time is under quota. In Canada and in certain other areas which produce wheat we have more or less come to an agreement that we will restrict the production of this essential food to the amount the market will absorb. I am not objecting to that, because under our present system it seems that that is the only way we can dispose of it, but I do want to say that any system based on that theory is wrong. In a world in which two-thirds of the population need more food, it seems ridiculous that we should have restricted the production of such an essential food as wheat. In the United States in the nineteen thirties they restricted the production of cotton, of corn, of hogs and other foods, and yet at the same time there were thousands of people in that country who were going without the necessary clothing, the necessary shoes and the necessary food to maintain a reasonable standard of living. Later they recognized the foolishness of that procedure and introduced the stamp plan for the distribution of food to those in the low income groups. I think the world should recognize that that is the most sensible thing to do. We should produce all the food we can and then see that it is distributed to the people who need it. If we want a world in which there will be permanent peace, I believe we will have to do that. You cannot have permanent peace in a world in which one part is restricting food production while another is starving to death. It is not Christianity, it is not economically sound, it is not common sense. It is one of the things I hope this organization will avoid. I hope they will make recommendations to the various governments to prevent it from taking place in the future.
Another matter on which this organization can make recommendations is agricultural credits. This has been one of the drawbacks to more efficient agricultural production throughout the world. The cost of credit for agricultural development, for the clearing of land, for obtaining proper equipment to work the land economically in order to get the best production, has been too great. The rates of interest charged throughout the world for agricultural credits have been unreasonable. In countries where agricultural credits have been made cheaper, there is greater production. I do not know whether

it is correct, but I am told that in India and in other countries where small acreages are worked, very often the people engaged in agriculture pay rates of interest of eight, ten and fifteen per cent. The result is that they are always in poverty and there is never the necessary production to meet the needs of the people.
t In Canada in the past few years we have been able to reduce the cost of credit to agriculture, and I think it can be still further reduced. Any recommendations which this organization may be able to make with respect to the obtaining or making available of cheaper agricultural credits will be all to the good.
Another matter on which they could make recommendations is land tenure, the method under which we hold our land. We think that with our individual ownership in Canada we have attained the best method of land ownership, but there are drawbacks to this system. I have followed agriculture pretty closely for the last forty years, and it seems to me that with our present system of ownership we have reduced the fertility of our soil. I know that in Ontario very few farms are producing what they produced fifty years ago, and in western Canada we find that our per acre production is being reduced. If we are holding our own, it is simply because we have developed better types of grain, not because we are maintaining the fertility of the soil.

The organization does not propose to standardize production or consumption throughout the world. There are entirely different methods that will have to be used in different countries. The money which we shall have to contribute to the expenses of the organization will be money well spent.
In conclusion I should like to quote what Mr. Appleby, the under-secretary of state of the United States, said with respect to this organization. After indicating that the organization was being developed for the purpose of obtaining a freedom-from-want programme in the world, he went on to say:

Whereas the first cause of hunger and malnutrition is poverty.

To maintain an equilibrium in balances of payments, and to achieve the orderly management of currencies and exchange.

That with a view to balancing production and consumption the permanent organization consider to what extent and by what means such reports might contribute to international collaboration both on a regional and on a world basis in the field of agricultural production.
That appears to me to relate to two things: First, distribution within the country, and, second, balancing exports with imports. It might be interesting at this point to emphasize to the house what foreign trade really should amount to. That is good stuff.

Since the house started, all parties have been working in a fine spirit of unity in order to find the solution of all our social and economic problems and as set out in bill No. 14.
Section 3 of the bill reads:
As soon as practicable after the close of each fiscal year the Secretary of State for External Aifairs shall prepare and lay before parliament a report of operations under this act.
The trouble is that we have been thinking too much in terms of "external affairs," with the result that we are more than two years behind the mother country in the adoption of proposals which would have led to an improved agriculture and food situation. What did they do in the mother country? The Hot Springs conference, as I have said, was attended by forty-four nations, and on July 6, 1943, the British government got out a white paper in which there appeared all the resolutions passed at the conference. The three objects of the conference were: first, to raise the level of nutrition and standards of living of the peoples in the respective jurisdictions; the second was to secure improvements in the efficiency of production and distribution of food and of agricultural products; and the third object of the forty-four nations was to better the conditions of rural populations, thus contributing toward an expanding world economy. On the same day on which Mr. Eden made his statement in the British House of Commons, July 6, 1943, we should have had a corresponding statement here the same day. We have lost more than two years by not adopting up-to-date methods in dealing with this subject. Let me quote what Mr. Eden, British Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, said that day.
His Majesty's government have no hesitation in accepting the resolutions and the obligation to give effect to them in so far as they apply to_ the conditions in the United Kingdom. They will also gladly cooperate with other governments in seeking ways to give effect to those resolutions which call for concerted action. They will commend the resolutions to the governments of His Majesty's colonies, dependencies and overseas territories.
The main object of the conference was to secure an abundant supply of the right kind of food for all mankind. World-wide investigations show, states the conference report,

that the diets consumed by the greater part of mankind are nutritionally unsatisfactory. The white paper continues:
Nutrition therefore becomes a primary concern of governments everywhere. To give conscious planned direction to mankind's need for food in the modern sense each nation should develop a national food and nutrition policy to the full fruition of which related social and economic policies will need to be adopted.
In my opinion that is correct. A famous Conservative, Mr. Disraeli, said that the first concern of the nation should be the health of the people. Speaking at Edinburgh in 1867 to the farmers of that district, he said:
In a progressive country change is constant; and the great question is, not whether you should resist change, which is inevitable, but whether the change should be carried out in deference to the manners, the customs, the laws, the traditions of the people, or in deference to abstract principles, and arbitrary and general doctrines.
He went on to say, that "power has only one duty, to secure the social welfare of the people." That was the utterance of a great humanitarian, Mr. Benjamin Disraeli, a prime minister of the mother country. His principles have been carried out by his successors, including the government of which Hon. Mr. Hudson was recently a member.
All men are consumers of food, the report says, and more than two-thirds of them are producers of it. Clearly, therefore, the nutrition policy and the agricultural policy of the nations must be considered interdependent. If the nutritional needs of mankind are to be satisfied, a vast increase in agricultural production will be necessary throughout the world; and producers must know not only what they have to do, but also that their labours will secure for them an adequate livelihood.
The conference supported this bill No. 14. It does not refer, however, to the method or manner of controls through orders in council. The conference indicated its conviction that the types of food needed to improve people's diets and health are in many cases those produced by methods of farming best calculated to keep the soil productive and to increase and stabilize the returns of the farmers. In short, better nutrition means better farming.
There is a summary of these main resolutions in the white paper. The first deals with intention:	governments should declare to
their own people their intention to secure more and better food for the people.
Next, post-war shortage, which was known in this house three or four years ago to be a practical certainty. The summary states that it was agreed that the period1 following the liberation of occupied countries would be one

of excessive scarcity. Governments, therefore, should work together to produce more food, especially cereals and other foods which promote energy and satisfy hunger, and to prevent, speculative and violent fluctuations in prices.
Immediate measures. The white paper says that while the ultimate objective must be a world in which all are fed adequately for good health, it will be necessary as a practical measure to concentrate on intermediate objectives which can be advanced as conditions improve.
The next clause of the resolutions of the food conference adopted in Britain relates to research, a matter which I urged on the minister back in 1938 in connection with reservoirs of food for the mother country. We should have taken full advantage of science and research. At that time the British medical association was meeting in London, and they pointed out that grain and canned and other goods could be stored at suitable food reservoirs in Great Britain for emergency purposes. The Hot Springs conference suggests that all nations should train scientific workers and rural leaders for service in agriculture and promote technical efficiency among producers by means of education and research. The nations should exchange with each other factual information and statistics regarding food and agriculture.
A world-wide economy is the subject of another resolution. A balanced worldi-wide expansion of economic activity must be achieved to secure freedom from want, since it is no use producing the food if the standard of living of the people is too low for them to buy it.
A permanent international organization such as is set out in bill No. 14 is proposed1, to collect and disseminate information and statistics regarding food and agriculture.
The British Minister of Agriculture, Mr. R. S. Hudson, with whom I once had some correspondence in reference to a food reservoir, said, speaking in the House of Commons on the same day that Mr. Eden announced the government's acceptance of the conference resolutions:
The recent conference at Hot Springs was attended by forty-four nations. That conference passed several resolutions which I think will prove to be of the greatest significance for agriculture throughout the world. These resolutions were passed unanimously. No delegations entered any reservations at all. Incidentally, it was the occasion of considerable tribute being paid to the British delegation under the leadership of the under secretary of state for foreign affairs.
That was Mr. Eden. On the subject of post-war food scarcities, the minister remarked:
One of the most striking facts which emerged from that conference was the general agreement that immediately after the war the world would be faced with an acute shortage of food, and that this shortage would cover not only actual foodstuffs, but would also cover methods of transportation, and methods of production, such as fertilizers, machinery, draft animals, petrol and so forth.
The British Minister of Agriculture continued:
It is, I think, clear that the industry of agriculture, at all events in this country, will have to remain fully mobilized for a period after the war which cannot be determined to-day. . . . What is clear, and what all the nations gathered at Hot Springs were clear and agreed about, is that, taking the world as a whole, there will undoubtedly be a severe shortage of live stock and live stock products, of oils and fats, and it is highly likely, difficult as it may seem to believe, that there will be an actual shortage of bread grains and of rice. The reasons for this shortage are obvious. A large part of the agriculture of Europe, Russia and Asia has been thrown into disorder and it will take a considerable period for those countries and those continents to get on their feet again.
It will be noticed that Russia has been called upon for a contribution of only eight per cent, which I think is very fair.
As to the production programmes:
The conference at Hot Springs recommended that all countries should plan their production programmes on a realistic basis and should concentrate on measures to relieve hunger in the first instance, even at the expense of putting nutritional improvements of diet second. They pointed out that it was necessary to concentrate on foodstuffs for direct human consumption. . . .
The conference also said that those countries, like ourselves, which have already increased food production during the war, must maintain that increased production and if possible increase it.
Speaking of the British policy, the minister said that they agreed with the resolutions re food production, and added:
We consider that the best contribution we can make to the food problems of the world is to continue producing from our own soil, food for as large a proportion as we can for as long as that process proves to be necessary.
For nearly a hundred years Britain has been dependent for her food supply very largely on imports from abroad. As a result of the government's recent policy they have expanded their own food production about seventy per cent since the war broke out, and have made a great contribution to the progress and security which the British farmer at present enjoys.

As to security for the farmer, I will read just one or two more sentences of this report:
What are the economic risks to which the farmer is subjected? In the first place, he is subject to wide fluctuations in prices, with the subsequent ups and down in the returns ... to fluctuations in employment, and to fluctuations in outputs, due to weather and outbreaks of disease. Clearly,- the more mixed farming you get, the less is your danger from those fluctuations, because you spread your risks over a greater number of products.
The conference stressed the point that all these economic and biological dangers can be greatly diminished by the adoption of systems of mixed rotational farming.
The minister goes on to say, referring to certain sections of hostile urban and politico-economic opinion:
Is it too much to hope that those people will note that forty-four nations, assembled at Hot Springs, unanimously decided that it was in the general interests of mankind that agriculture should be based on sound fundamental principles, and those fundamental principles involve the maintenance of soil fertility and a system of mixed . . . farming.
The last resolution which is referred to deals with price stability:
There is another resolution to which I should, in fairness, call attention, which says that increasing opportunities should be afforded for supplying consumption needs at prices fair to both producers and consumers alike, to prevent serious economic and social dislocation.
The resolution states that excessive shortterm movements in prices of food and agricultural products are an obstacle to the orderly development of production, that extreme fluctuations of prices of food and agricultural products increase inflationary and also deflationary tendencies, and that these tendencies harm producers and consumers alike.
As to the world policy which has been decided upon for agriculture, this resolution sets out-and we are a party to it when we pass this bill-that the Hot Springs resolution definitely pointed the way to a world policy for agriculture, first of all for the short-term period of acute shortage and then a new period of gradual adjustment; then finally, they laid down the basic principles on which a practical policy for a well balanced agriculture could be carried out throughout the world. If these policies outlined at Hot Springs are followed and put into effect in each country according to its different economic conditions we shall, I think, have gone a long way along the road to solving the problems which faced primary producers throughout the world in pre-war days.
This interim commission was formed at the Hot Springs conference to formulate and recommend for consideration by each member

government or authority a specific plan for a permanent organization in the field of food and agriculture, and the commission's first report has been published in the form of a white paper, in 1945. The British government's instrument of acceptance is signed by Mr. Eden and dated December 14, 1944. That is the policy laid down there. In 1943 Mr. Churchill said:
Abundant food has brought our 47.000,000 Britons into the world. Here they are, and they must find their living. It is absolutely certain we shall have to grow a larger proportion of our food at home. During the war immense advances have been made by the agricultural industry. The position of the farmers has been improved; the position of the labourers immeasurably improved. The efficient agricultural landlord has an important part to play. I hope to see a vigorous revival of healthy village life on the basis of these higher wages and of improved housing after the war, and what with the modern methods of locomotion and the modern amusements of the cinema and the wireless, to wdiich will soon be added television, life in the country and on the land ought to compete in attractiveness with life in the great cities.
So that they have increased their production by seventy per cent.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to refer to the method the government has adopted in this case; that is, the method of carrying on by order in council, even after the war is over. As you know there was a great deal of criticism in this country during the war because of the way government was carried on by order in council. Knowing it was for the war, however, the people gladly gave up many of their rights and privileges which it took hundreds of years to secure. This matter was referred to this afternoon by the hon. member for Lake Centre. One of the great contributions the mother country has made to the history of the world and to civilization is the ideal of a community of free men governing themselves through a free parliament, such as we had in Canada before the war started. To-day, however, we almost take for granted many of the liberties which have been given to us during the last three hundred years. Let us think of the great struggle that was carried on to secure those rights and privileges. Remember the struggle carried on by the barons against King John. After all is said and done, it was the armed strength of the barons that made magna charta possible. Now, however, under measures like this we are giving up some of the liberties and privileges won at such great cost.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. In this connection I would refer to the Book of Revelations, to quote a verse which is relevant to this discussion:
Behold, I come quickly: hold that fast which thou hast, that no man take thy crown.

If it goes on much longer I do not want to be a member of parliament, because I do not want to see my rights and privileges taken away, and the institutions to which I have referred forgotten and abandoned. Men suffered at the stake to win these liberties for us, and we must not lightly drop them. This House of Commons is the court of last resort for the grievances of the people, and tihe private member is the connecting link between the government of the day and the electors. When he ceases to function, as he has had to cease functioning in this house during the war, free parliaments and parliamentary government is at an end.
With all due respect I repeat that I object to the method and manner by which this particular measure is to be carried into effect by orders in council. I do not believe it is necessary. The minister would be far better off to support the high court of parliament, as they have done in the mother country, and put a sum of money in the estimates to be passed each year. Heaven knows that in a rich country like Canada, where we had no invasion, where no buildings were destroyed and no damage done, we are in a very favourable position.
