I urge that this instrument is worthy of unanimous ratification by this parliament, and I need mention only two reasons. In the first place this agreement should receive the greatest possible support because it is based upon humanitarian considerations. The feeding of the hungry in all parts of the world is and must be of concern to the people of this enlightened, Christian land. It is something of which we as Canadians should be proud that we can take a very important part in that great work. In the next place this agreement ought to command the widest support because it represents an important step in the field of international relations. It is an agreement among nations. We in Canada are looking for opportunities to assist in giving leadership throughout the world in relations between nations. Here we have the field of the production of foodstuffs in which Canada holds a position of leadership. Therefore it is only right and proper that in the negotiating an agreement and in implementing of an agreement in relation to the feeding of the peoples of the world Canada should have a leading part.	_
In the past we have done much for which we might reproach ourselves. Let it not be forgotten that we, along with some of the other food producing nations of the world, in days not so long removed, were busy reducing production and in some cases destroying foodstuffs at a time when millions of people throughout the world starved. Surely we have taken a step, a long step, from that discreditable situation. This agreement offers an opportunity to take a long step away from that discreditable episode of our past.
Let it not be thought that in helping to raise the standard of living among other nations of the world we are doing anything to reduce the standard of living of our own people-far from it. The surest guarantee of the betterment of the standard of living of our own people will be the betterment of the standard of living of those vast millions of people the world over who to-day have not enough to eat.
Can we ponder what it would mean to Canada, in safeguarding our standard of living, if the hungry millions of Asia, who some day may be competing with us for the world's markets, had as high a standard of living as we have?

the maintenance of the standard of living of her people at home, lies in this urgent need- and perhaps in other respects as well-that we must help other nations to raise their standard of living. This measure gives an opportunity to Canada to help in that worthy cause.
I suggest that measures of this type are the kind upon which we should like and ought to see parliament expressing its views in unanimous terms. It is a matter of disappointment, therefore, that the bill now before us presents this agreement in such a way that those of us who are determined to oppose arbitrary measures find that iwe must criticize the bill and criticize it strongly. It would have been so much better, I suggest, both for the effect at home and for the effect abroad, had it been possible to put this agreement before parliament for simple ratification, without at the same time introducing sections which are calculated to give the government the most sweeping powers, powers which a self-respecting parliament in a time like this cannot transfer to a cabinet.
It is a matter of disappointment that we have not the opportunity, as the bill stands to-night, to express ourselves unanimously in support of the ratification of the measure. There are one or two things which might properly be said to the government at this time, and which might prevent a repetition in connection with later measures which will come before the house.
Our experience in Canada in recent years with government by order in council has put at least those of us who sit on this side of the house, on our guard with respect to arbitrary measures. It has not served to allay our fears or our suspicions when, in the five and one-half weeks parliament has been in session, the government has continued to legislate by order in council and apparently under the authority of the War Measures Act with reference to subjects which have no connection whatsoever with the war.
It is against that background that we propose to survey all the measures the government introduces at this session. The government might as well understand right now that we propose to bring critical views to bear upon those government measures. I repeat that we are on our guard against arbitrary measures. We have had so much bureaucracy in recent years that we are on our guard against the creation of more of it, or the perpetuation of existing bureaucracy.
It is no comfort to the house to have the government point to some measures which were passed in parliaments of other years and which contain language similar to that found

in section 2 of the bill. That is no comfort. It may be that the parliament which was in session when those measures were adopted was a parliament which felt that the government of that day, on its assurances and on its record, could be entrusted with certain powers to proceed by way of orders in council to implement the provisions of international treaties.
That situation does not obtain at the present time. Our position on this side of the house is that there shall be the strictest scrutiny applied to government measures, and the strongest opposition voiced to anything which proposes the extension of the powers of the government to legislate by order in council.
I suggest that, above all other kinds of measures with which we may have to deal in this parliament, measures affecting international relations ought to be kept squarely within the ambit of the powers of parliament, and that those in relation to international agreements ought not to seek to take from parliament and vest in a cabinet powers which normally would be exercised by parliament itself.
The reason for that position is obvious. Here we are dealing, not with something which affects only our own citizens, but with something which affects our relations with other nations of the world, some of the leading nations of the world. Our relations with those nations may be affected by the course followed with respect to the agreement with which we are attempting to deal in the measure before us to-night.
In these circumstances, if Canada means to fulfil her obligations and to fulfil the pledges contained in her international agreements, it is vital that such measures should command the most widespread support within Canada and within parliament. Above all other measures they should be the last to seek to take from parliament powers which are properly vested in parliament. How else can we ensure that solid foundation of public support and that necessary measure of success for these international agreements, and the permanence of international relations which we mean to seek?
Very briefly, I wish to compare this measure with one or two others which were adopted in earlier parliaments. I suggest that the comparison will be decidedly to the disadvantage of the present measure. I draw attention, in the first place, to the fact that in this measure we are not being invited to ratify in express terms the international agreement. We are not being asked to ratify the agreement. Let no one think that there is one section in the bill which is, in express terms, a ratification of the agreement, because that is not so.

Mark you, authorized by parliament.
-to advise that His Majesty be humbly moved to ratify on behalf of Canada the said protocol of the sixteenth day of December, 1920, in the manner thereby stipulated.

There is another phase of the matter which I do not intend to deal with at any length because it was so ably dealt with this afternoon by the hon. member for Lake Centre. Section 2 of this bill is a most extraordinary piece of draftsmanship. Certainly the draftsman of this legislation was schooled in the school of bureaucracy which has flourished at Ottawa in recent years, because this is on all fours with the kind of legislation which has been ground out by parliament in recent years. Under that section the governor in council is authorized, not only to make appointments, establish offices, pass orders in
council and do whatever things may appear to him to be necessary to carry out the provisions of the constitution; he is to be granted those powers in connection with the recommendations of the conference of the food and agricultural organization.

Mr. Speaker, I rise wtih a great deal of pleasure to speak in favour of this bill with which I am in sympathy. The bill, which is to establish an agricultural organization of the united nations, recognizes one great thing, namely, that to-day many nations of the world believe in a world citizenship. Such a bill would never have come before this parliament twenty-five years ago, but since then we have passed through one of the most crucial stages in the world's history and have fought a global war. The bill recognizes that to-day all countries have a responsibility to other countries throughout the world and must have regard to the rights and needs of other peoples. I consider this a Christian responsibility.
There has been a good deal of discussion of the bill and some controversy has developed over the maintenance of controls, but the very fact that we live in a country where we are more fortunate than peoples in other parts of the world does impose upon us a definite responsibility. It is not enough to put on paper or even to inaugurate a system of world organization unless we are ready to make fundamental changes, and in the few moments at my disposal I shall mention some fundamental changes which I believe are necessary.
One of the big questions which this parliament has to decide is whether we are to have a high or a low income in Canada. During the war, in 1943, we had a gross income of $8,800,000,000, and according to the bureau of statistics that is about sixty-eight per cent over the 1926-29 level. There has been some intimation from members of the cabinet that in order to have full employment or anywhere near it in this country labour would have to take a cut-back of from twenty-five to forty per cent. We have also been told by various ministers that agriculture must be satisfied with lower returns for its products. I should like to quote what the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said, as reported at page 425

May I say in conclusion that we have made exactly the same kind of arrangement with regard to cattle. That contract extends down to December 31, 1946. We have been told that we have unemployment insurance and family allowances, but after all the sacrifices the Canadian people made in war I do not think they will be satisfied with that kind of floor under our Canadian economy, and so I am going to submit that we need a fundamental change. We have had in this country a government which does not believe in planning. They have said so themselves. Yet through the sheer necessity of planning to meet our war commitments we have been able to increase our natural production from around three billions to approximately nine billions of dollars. Therefore I maintain that if we launch upon a system of high income in Canada we can maintain a high level of income for all our people. The fight is not between the farmer and labour, because we in this group have shown to the people that we are interdependent. We have shown that if we can take the resources of this country and can put our people to work on them we can produce a wealth of things. What we produce on our farms and in our factories represents wealth and the social services that we can provide for ourselves. What we export in the way of surpluses means that we thereby build up credits or else we import. The fact is, as it has been in the past, that unless we import as much as we export, the Canadian people are short by just that amount of foodstuffs and other commodities. The first thing we should realize, and as a farmer from western Canada I certainly realize it, is that a larger income in the hands of the workers means a larger consumption of the products of the farm. More purchasing power in the hands of the workers means that they will buy more butter, cheese, eggs, pork and other farm products. Those of us who live in western Canada need farm machinery and various other goods. Therefore to-day we should start our factories going, producing the machinery that is required by the western ;farmer and by farmers all over Canada.
One of the first things we must do in order to establish Canadian domestic economy on a sound basis is to establish it on a high income basis. Then we can meet our Christian commitments, if you like, to the united nations. We can join with the other nations who are willing to recognize their responsibilities to all countries of the world to-day to feed and clothe the starving and destitute who are less fortunate than ourselves. Surely we realize to-day that it is much cheaper and much better to share than to hoard surpluses which may lead us into another war. The leader of this group said at one time, not what Napoleon said, that an army marches on its stomach, but that armies march when their stomachs are empty. I am in agreement with that. When we have starving millions in Europe and Asia, unless we do something about it we shall have trouble.
I should like to read into the record something regarding the lack of stability in this country and the need for some sort of planning. Some of the opposition members have criticized the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, and one hon. member said that we would not agree with what he was saying when he was decrying the fact that this bill would necessitate orders in council, involving a lack of power on the part of this parliament. Let me say that we have never at any time said anything against democracy. We believe in democracy and in the rights of this parliament. At the same time we recognize that orders in council, and some of the actions of the cabinet, produce what one might call "funny" things. Certainly we do not want any situation to exist such as has been described in my own constituency. A certain man went everywhere looking for underwear in the middle of the winter. He went to every town within his reach and all he could get was one suit. He needed underclothing and so did his son, but it happened that the father's shoulders were cold while most of the son's trouble was in his lower extremities, and so they cut the suit in two, each using one-half of it. That is not what we want. We want carefully considered planning so that what we have done for war we can do for peace.
In closing, let me say that I heartily endorse the principle of this responsibility which the bill recognizes.

I wish to make a few observations on the bill before the house. In the first place, it appears to be allinclusive, but because it has a direct relationship to agriculture I feel that it commends itself to our serious consideration.

United Nations Food Agreement
I look upon agriculture as one of the great basic industries of the country, an industry from which we derive much of our wealth. In fact, it is the one dependable source of real wealth we have in Canada. I am thinking now of our basic industries-agriculture, forestry, fishery and our mines. The bill has a direct relationship to each of these, and therefore I think that since it has these potentialities it should receive the favourable consideration of hon. members.
Then, too, its human character must not be overlooked. It will indeed play an important part in contributing to the solution of a great problem, that of distributing our agricultural products to the distant corners of the earth, particularly if those whose names appear at the end of the bill become members of this great organization. So I say that a bill which seeks to introduce some measure whereby we can in an orderly fashion distribute the products of our fields, our forests and our streams will indeed play an important part in the future economy of the nations.
I feel, however, that a certain amount of criticism can be offered and I have listened with interest to the observations made by my colleagues who have preceded me. I have recognized, in the limited time it has been my privilege to serve in this house, a tendency to introduce measures at a time when the element of haste is always attendant upon their presentation. Indeed, this is no exception to the rule, inasmuch as I think this has happened time and again. As a matter of fact, this bill is brought in for second reading on the very eve of royal assent, so that we are in a position where we must deal with a measure far-reaching in its import, having possibly great effects; and yet I doubt whether we have the time to consider properly the various articles of the agreement.
I should like to see some provision in the oill requiring that the various signatories or representatives of the countries involved

I suppose it must be approached in its broadest application-shall have to report to their respective governments so that the peoples' representatives may have an opportunity to view and review the contributions being made by the various members of the organization.
Do we realize that in our haste, from our lack of consideration, we may be delegating to some authority responsibilities which are primarily ours and which we may not easily reclaim? I have always taken strong exception to anything savouring of totalitarianism, and yet the very provisions of the bill seem, in my opinion, to be -rather far-reaching, because we become members of the organization for a period of five years, or, to be more

precise, four years with one year's notice in the case of withdrawal. I say, therefore, that we may be delegating authority to some organization which we shall no longer be able to control.
As a matter of fact, I believe that a commitment for five years is too long; it savours of the closed shop, which was debated in this house recently. I should like to know from the minister when he replies what was the basis of assessment in determining the contribution to be made by the various nations. In annex II to the bill, giving the budget for the first financial year, I read:
The provisional budget for the first financial year shall be a sum of 2.500.000 U.S. dollars, the unspent balance of which shall constitute the nucleus of a capital fund.
This sum shall be contributed by the member nations in the following proportions.
Then the different percentages are set out, and if my arithmetic is correct, Canada's contribution will be $126,500; Great Britain's, $375,000; and the United States' $625,000. Then it appears to be intimated that the over-all total required in the next year will be $5 million. While I do not find fault with that, I should like some explanation from the minister and an opportunity to go into the matter more thoroughly.

I had not intended to rise on this second reading, since we are discussing only the principle of the -bill, but in view of some of the statements which have been made, probably the position of the members of our party should be made clear.
First, since this bill aims to establish on an international level some controls whereby people throughout the world may be properly fed, we support the principle, as, I believe, do hon. members in every part of the house. A start has been made in real cooperation between the various peoples. Nations must learn to cooperate and look upon one another as brothers. Causes of wars are very closely related to problems of want. This international conference aims to do away with want. Modern science as exemplified in the atomic bomb has made it abundantly clear that, unless the world can end wTars, wars will end us.
This conference also aims to do away with some obstacles which in the past have prevented the rank and file everywhere from receiving proper food. That is a great objective. We support these aims 100 per cent.
During the speech of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) this afternoon, he gave some figures which demonstrated the tremendous extent of malnutrition and undernourishment. I wondered whether he had

United Nations Food Agreement
made any analysis of the causes of this condition. We in this great country of ours, composing nearly half a continent and containing only eleven and a half million people, and one of the greatest food producers in the world, find these conditions of malnutrition and want here at home. Coming from the western prairies, I have seen instances which illustrate this. A boy about twelve or thirteen years of age came to town and. walked into a store with five or six pounds of butter which, by herding, feeding and milking cows, he had helped to produce. He was selling that butter. From his appearance one could see that he was undernourished. I asked him if he ever ate any butter, and he said, "no." "In fact," he said, "we have to sell our butter." I said, "Why?" "Well," he said, "I am sent into town this afternoon with this butter which we have produced, and the purpose of selling it is to buy machinery repairs." The prices of the things which the farmer must buy lie beyond his control. When he comes to purchase some commodity he must pay what he is told is the price, but when he comes to sell something he is told1 the price at which it shall be sold, and the incomes of those who actually produce the wealth of the nation are so low that they cannot afford adequate food. As has been said this afternoon, the cause of malnutrition and undernourishment is poverty; and I contend that this conference will have to make some basic changes in the world economy before it will succeed in feeding the worlds peoples. We support that objective.
The statement was made this afternoon by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group could not oppose the setting up of boards by orders in council. I deny that statement completely. This group has been maintaining that orders in council should never be used in peace time for establishing arbitrarily any boards. If any group in ithis house stands for democracy it is the CC.F. group, the one group whose programme and policy and party are based on democratic annual conferences.
Since when? Your party are more dictatorial in British Columbia than anybody else.

You can tell your
little story later. We have listened to you for many years. When did you hold your last convention, 1919?
I do not need any convention.
Order.
lit is just a waste of time.

Section 2 of this bill as it stands should be opposed by every person who objects to the granting of unlimited powers by order in council in the hands of the government. That section states:
(1) The governor in council may make such appointments, establish such offices, make such orders in council and do such things as appear to him to be necessary for carrying out the provisions of the constitution set out in the schedule to this act or any recommendations of the conference of the food and agriculture organization of the united nations, or of its committees made pursuant to such provisions.
How can we be satisfied with the carrying out by order in council of any recommendation which may be presented by future organizations and future councils over which we have no control? We believe that under war conditions orders in council may be necessary, but whatever boards are set up and whatever actions are taken by order in council require to be ratified by this parliament. I wanted to make that point clear.

If there is no other hon. member who wishes to speak on this motion, the mover, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) will have the floor, but it is understood that, as the mover, he will close the debate.

Mr. Speaker, I wish in the

With regard to that I can only say that I have before me at the moment the resolution passed by the United States under the heading "Joint resolution providing for membership of the United States in the food and agricultural organizations of the United Nations." Then follows a resolution in five short sections, approved July 31, 1945. That is, the nation which is responsible for a greater part of the expense than any other nation involved, namely twenty-five per cent. The next largest contributor, the United Kingdom, is responsible for fifteen per cent. The United Kingdom, the second largest contributor to the expenses of the organization did not, so far as I have been able to find, pass legislation with regard to this matter. The British government apparently has much greater authority than the parliament of Canada has ever seen fit to give to the government of Canada; and I am not critical of the parliament of Canada when I make that statement. My understanding is that



United Nations Food Agreement
bill by order in council, without its first being passed upon by the House of Commons, in carrying out the recommendation made by this organization at any time.
I think all hon. members will agree that if we are to be a party to the conference, then provision ought to be made in the bill, and it ought to be understood, that in so far as making provision for the actual administration costs is concerned, we are to pay our share in accordance with the constitution which was set up. Are we to say to the other nations that are going into the organization at the present time that we are not prepared for the four years ahead of us to pay our share of the administration costs which have been set up in t>'e articles which constitute the constitution I am sure hon. members would not wish so to state.
I agree with what was said by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), that the sum of money set up is a small sum, compared with the great amount of good which could come to Canada and to other nations of the world through the expenditure of $126,500 in the first year and a sum no greater than $253,000 in the years thereafter.
From what I have heard this afternoon and this evening I think the house will be quite prepared to have the undertaking given that that amount of money is available. I understand the intention of the house, and particularly that of the official opposition is that they do not desire to have any money made available by the government of Canada for the carrying out of the recommendations which may be made by the conference, in order to assist in any undertaking which they think should be proceeded with, without its first being passed upon by the parliament of Canada.
My understanding, too, is that they feel that when orders in council are passed they should be placed upon the table of the house at as early a day as possible. I think hon. members who have sat here during the ten years in which I have been a member will agree that in no case has the government refused to bring down orders in council and place them upon the table of the house, except in those comparatively few cases during the war period, when that was not possible. But as soon as it did become possible, under the conditions of war then existing, such orders in council were always placed upon the table of the house.
We have no reason whatsoever for taking any different action in connection with this particular matter. In so far as reports are concerned, we are quite prepared to have the section which deals with the making of returns
[Mr. Gardiner.)
to the house changed to read in almost any way hon. members of the opposition may desire to have it read. But in my own opinion -and that may not be worth much-I think it is much stronger mow than it would be if we were to insert the terms suggested during the discussion.
For example, it says:
As soon as practicable after the close of each fiscal year, the Secretary of State for External Affairs shall prepare and lay before parliament a report of operations under this act.
My understanding of the requirement related to most of the reports which have to do with my own department is that I must lay on the table of the house within fifteen days after the opening of the next session of parliament the last report brought out. Sometimes that is almost twelve months away. It may be six months, eight months or a longer period of time. But this section says:

I believe the house, under that section, could hold the department to bringing down a report just as soon as it is available. If someone wishes to suggest that the report should be down within fifteen days from the opening of the next session, I do not know why hon. members on this side of the house should object to it. Again I say we are in the hands of the committee, and without any difficulty we can draft these sections to satisfy everyone who is in the house. Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
Section 1 agreed to.
On section 2-Powers of governor in council to carry out agreement.

I am sure the members of the committee have listened with interest to the remarks of the mover of this bill. Personally I wish to compliment him upon the attitude he has taken. Those of us on this side of the committee have to take the bill as we received it, and we criticized it because it did not provide for the presenting of a report or that orders in council be presented. We felt that section 2 gave wider powers than were necessary. I think the Minister of Agriculture has taken a fair attitude with respect to those criticisms. The hon. member (Mr. Diefenbaker) who sits behind me will have some amendments to

The budget for the financial year is set out in the schedule and at the end is given the percentages which will be contributed by the different nations. Canada's contribution is to be 5-06 per cent; Australia's is to be 3-33 per cent; Russia's, 8 per cent; the United Kingdom, 15 per cent, and the United States ' of America, 25 per cent. How were those percentages arrived at? Why has a country such as Russia, which is as large as the United States, been asked to contribute only 8 per cent as against our five per cent?

The only answer I can give is that these matters were all discussed very fully by the representatives of all the nations who were present at the conference. In reply to something said a few moments ago by the hon. member for Broadview, I may say that the questions we discussed this afternoon were discussed in our own agriculture committee and in this house shortly after he Hot Springs gathering. I assume that the representatives of the forty-four nations who were at that conference came to the conclusion that these proportions were what should be asked from each of the nations gathered there at that time. Our representative, along with the others, agreed to the proportions. The United States bears the highest proportion of 25 per cent; the United Kingdom, 15 per cent; the U.S.S.R., 8 per cent; France, 5-69 per cent; China, 6-5 per cent, and then we come in with 5-06 per cent. The only answer I can give is that this was agreed to at the conference at Hot Springs and that we are committed to it by the suggestions that have been made.

That does not answer my question. I think the committee is entitled to know just how these percentages were arrived at. There must have been some basis. Take China with 6-5 per cent. China has a large population but very little to give at the present time. The percentage for India is 4-25 per cent, while Canada's is 5-06 per cent, as against 8 per cent for Russia.

sion where there is an explanation of the allocation of the costs. Perhaps that will supplement the minister's answer.

The constitution of this-international organization describes it as the food and agriculture organization of the united nations. In the preamble to bill No. 14 now before the committee we find the words:
... to prepare a plan for a permanent international organization for food and agriculture. . . .
I point out that the reference there also is-to food and agriculture; the same words are-used throughout in both the constitution and the bill. However, in article XVI of the constitution we find:
In this constitution the term "agriculture"' and its derivatives include fisheries, marine products, forestry, and primary forestry products.
It would seem that by including forestry and forestry products the constitution goes far beyond what the public believe to be the purposes of this organization; that is, to dleal with food and agriculture. It may be that careful consideration has been given to the extent of that definition, but this is of great importance to my province of British Columbia because forestry is our major industry. The provincial government deals primarily with that industry and the federal government has very little power over it. I should like to know whether this matter of including forestry and forestry products has been discussed with the provincial governments and why it is the constitution is so broad.

When the proposals
came back from Hot Springs I raised the same question, and that was some two years ago. When the proposals came back this time I raised the same question. I am forced to the conclusion, by the explanations I got and by doing a little further thinking, that avery considerable part of the food of the world comes from what might be called, forestry. If we think in terms of coconuts, bananas, oranges and all the different fruits-that come from tree production; when we think of blights that attack trees and realize-that they attack fruit trees as well as ordinary forest trees, that is apparent. It is the-same staffs and individuals in all countries who deal with all matters that have to do-with the destruction of insects that destroy trees and plants and- everything of that kind..
I think that is the chief reason why forestry' is brought in under this measure. Measures-must be taken to protect food, and it was-thought proper to extend the activities to' forestry in its other meaning, as well as

forestry as related to food. The question of fisheries is self-evident because it is food practically altogether.

Have there been any discussions with the provincial governments concerning the fact that this constitution covers forestry and forestry products which to the layman means primarily lumber and logs and not fruit trees?

The discussions with the provincial governments have been related only to food, but I think I am correct in saying that the discussions vdiich will take place at this conference will be much broader because of the questions which the hon. member for Vancouver South knows have been put so often in the house in relation to the different insects that attack forest life in British Columbia and elsewhere. But it will be more definitely related to their effects upon food.

If the minister will refer to sections 56, 57, 58 and 59 of the first report of the interim commission he will see that whoever drew up this report had in mind going a good deal further than just dealing with pests, and I suggest to the ministry that careful consideration should be given to these suggestions as to what can be done by this international organization with regard to our forests. I think there is a great deal of doubt whether it is wise to go that far.

The amount of expenditure in support of a very worthy cause is nothing compared with that what we expect the returns will be, but when the sponsor of this bill was asked an important question, why a country of twelve millions of people should be paying five per cent against Russia's eight per cent-Russia, a countiy of one hundred and seventy millions of people-he told us that this subject was discussed in committees and in this house, and it did not seem to strike him that this was not a fair apportionment. He could not give a satisfactory answer. I think that point should be looked into before the bill is passed.

Probably I ought to
read the section referred to by the leader of the opposition since hon. members, seem to desire full information. It reads as follows:
The commission has found it difficult to devise a wholly satisfactory scale of apportionment of expenses.
They seem to have had the same thought in mind as the hon. member, that it was difficult to apportion the expenses. They went on to say:
It has considered whether such a scale might be formulated, based on such factors as capacity to pay modified, e.g., by the desirability of
IMr. Gardiner.]
maximum and minimum limits to contributions, the importance of agricultural production, national income, foreign trade, etc. If this could have been done and if world conditions were normal, such a scale might have been adopted by the conference for an indefinite period, or, at least, for the five-year period referred to above. The abnormal circumstances created by war and enemy occupation, however, and the impossibility of knowing when they will terminate, render it impossible to formulate a scale which is likely to be regarded as satisfactory except for a very short period. During the first or second year the conference probably will wish to consider, in the light of the conditions then prevailing, the equity of the scale which the commission now recommends. This scale, recommended for temporary use, is based upon a relationship among the member nations growing out of that accepted by them in respect of pre-war international organizations, but adjusted as follows:
(a)	the assumption of 54-5 per cent of the allocations by the United States, the United Kingdom, the Soviet Union, and China.
I explained to the house in my opening remarks this afternoon that these four nations should not be asked to pay more than 54-5 per cent. Then (b):
(b)	The scaling down of the allocations, as a measure of temporary financial relief, for those countries that are occupied by the enemy, or that have, in consequence of the war, suffered from major economic disasters.

The result of (b) and (c) has been substantially to increase the temporary allocations to the remaining countries. When world conditions improve, the proportions allocated to these countries will have to be correspondingly reduced.
Those are the reasons they give. I gave that in general terms myself a few moments ago.

What kind of committee is Canada going to set up to collect these foodstuffs in this country to be sent to other countries? Under Mutual Aid there was a committee that looked after the purchases and designated the firms to sell the stuff or give it to the other countries. What is in mind here?

Under Mutual Aid what happened ini regard to food products was this. We entered into agreements, practically all with Britain, to take our surplus foods and utilize them in any way they thought fit in the prosecution of the war in Europe. That in general terms related to our surplus foods. The means taken were not to bring together

aH these different products through any organization set up by us. We simply said to the people who were in the business, in connection with meat, for example, the packing plants, the drovers, and everybody else interested in bringing live stock together at certain places to have it processed: you just go ahead with the job as you did before, gather all this food in and have it processed and put in such a form that we can take it and have it delivered at certain ports. Then Britain gent her ships and took it away. That was the process followed in war. I do not expect that we shall require to follow any different procedure during the transition period covered by the next four or five years.
I should like to refer to a remark which was made a few moments ago to the effect that the government is for the first time planning. I think hon. members on both sides will agree when I say that we have never had a government in Canada that did not plan. It did not make any difference whether it was a Conservative or a Liberal government-and they have all been one or the other-we never had at any time a government that did not believe in planning. Every government has planned. This government has planned. We have done our planning all through this war, just as we did before the war. Some may differ as to the results we obtained from the planning, but all will agree that all governments have planned. For the period immediately following the war our plan has been that which was set out in what we call the floor price legislation passed by the last parliament. Under that legislation we say that so long as the people who are engaged in business can find markets for our products at reasonable prices, we are not going to interfere with them at all. That to all intents and purposes is what we say. We say that if the wheat board as now constituted, or some other organization if at some future time some government decides that wheat should be marketed in some other way and sets up an organization for the purpose, privately or through government, is able to find markets where the prices compare reasonably with the prices we have obtained, we shall not interfere. But if they are not able to do that; for example, if there are people starving in some parts of the world who are not able to pay for surplus food products that we are not able to dispose of, we say to them: We want that surplus disposed of in certain ways. They may say to us: We can handle that for you but we cannot handle it at a loss or we would go out of business. Then under the terms of that legislation we say to them: Well, you proceed to deliver the goods where they are required, and we will utilize the $200
million fund that has been made available under the legislation to take care of the difference between what you receive and what it was necessary to pay in order to maintain the price levels we think proper in this country. That is the method which I think would be followed in order to see to it that some of these countries, if conditions are such that they cannot pay, would be provided for. We would probably provide for some of their needs in some such way or through arranging credits with them under which they could buy our products under certain set prices.

The minister said he
would call in all producers. That is what was done under Mutual Aid. Under Mutual Aid you called in producers and you asked companies to submit prices although they had never even produced the goods. They had never produced the goods, had never even shipped to Britain, and I know that in the case of rolled oats you called in the different companies and some companies quoted prices although they had never shipped one ounce of rolled oats to Britain. They were asked to tender and they did tender and received contracts. Rolled oats were shipped to Britain, and instead of the government allowing one firm that had shipped to Britain practically all the rolled oats

packaged rolled oats-which Britain ever used, they allowed firms that had never sent over any to send inferior oats. To-day we in Canada have lost the British trade for these rolled oats. I will not mention the name, but one firm spent over $3 million in advertising before the war. They advertised their rolled oats in Britain, every sign board being plastered with their name, so that the people in Britain knew their product and knew there was nothing better in the world. But this government allowed other oats to go over and gave that firm a very small portion of the contract. That is what I am afraid of now under this arrangement, that we may lose other markets for other goods unless a great deal more consideration is given to the manufacturer and also the producer of food products here in Canada.

If I used the phrase
"called in"-

I think those are the
words.

-I did not intend to use that phrase or to give that impression. What I thought I said was that we called upon those who were in the business to continue to purchase and supply products. I am quite sure the hon. member for Peter-

Sborough West will agree with me when I say that the government would be very much criticized if we started going around the country picking out different companies and asking them either to submit prices or to do certain things in relation to supplying food products. What we actually do is to submit the proposition to the people of the country generally. We say, we want everyone to assist in supplying food who can possibly assist. It may be true that a company may express its intention of trying to supply a product although probably it had never supplied it before, but I cannot think of many cases where that happened during war time. Take, for example, in connection with bacon products, which is the big item that has been handled in that way. I do not remember their ever having made a complaint to me- and they discussed the situation with me many times-that they had difficulties with anyone in Canada who had supplied a product from here, but I understand that they had difficulties with some persons or some organizations who were supplying oatmeal on the other side, and they thought that market which had been built up by them in Britain was being utilized under war conditions by someone else who was supplying the product. My understanding was that that was a company not in Canada but elsewhere. I believe that difficulty was overcome in the latter part of the war. It developed only somewhere in the middle of it. A similar difficulty has arisen since the war was over, but that has nothing to do with any company in Canada, I understand, but with the desire of some organizations in Britain to have control of that market, if I understand the matter correctly. I would only say with regard to the direct question, that it would be very diffii-cult for us to go around the country selecting concerns and saying, you are better at this than somebody else and therefore you do it. rMr. Gardiner.]
We must say to anyone who wishes to enter the trade that he can enter, but we must insist that he provide a commodity which is up to the standard.

That is the point I was
trying to make, that the government should insist that we send over only the very best so that we can retain the markets we have already established, especially in bacon. The minister is just as much afraid as the farmers in Canada that Denmark will try to steal that trade from us again.

I listened with considerable interest to the speech of the Minister of Agriculture. There is one question he did not answer, and I should like to ask him a question before I propose to take advantage of the invitation he has given for suggestions regarding amendments. I asked him a question regarding the Argentine in view of the fact that that nation is one of the world's largest exporters of food products, and without that nation as a member of the nations comprised within this agreement, there might be obvious difficulties. The minister indicated that any nation could voluntarily assume membership in this organization, but that is not the position at all. Article II provides in subsection 2:
Additional members may be admitted to the organization by a vote concurred in by a two-thirds majority of all the members of the conference and upon acceptance of this constitution as in force at the time of admission.
I wish to ask the minister now, first, has Argentina given any indication of its desire to join in this conference? Second, if so, what is to be the attitude of the Canadian government toward such application? After the minister has answered that, if I may, I intend to suggest an amendment to paragraph 2.
I tried to answer it in making my reply. I am not sure whether the hon. member for Lake Centre was in the house at the time.
Yes, I was here.

I take from his remarks, then, that he does not accept as a complete answer the suggestion that I presume the Argentine could have made application when the forty-four nations met. It is not within my memory as to whether it did or did not at that particular time.

Has it done so
since?

I do not know that it
has, since. I would assume that if the Argentine had expressed the desire to be there at that time, or had been there, it would have

United Nations Food Agreement
been considered along with others. My statement a few minutes ago was that a nation would have voluntarily to indicate its desire to come in before anyone would expect them to come; there would be and could be no compulsion used. But I can understand why they might wish to have acceptance of a nation depend upon a two-thirds vote. I assume they anticipate that, as time goes on, some of the nations which we have been recently fighting will make application, and that others associated with them will make application. They may want to consider all the circumstances concerning those cases at that time, as to whether they shall admit them or not, and they may believe that they should have a two-thirds majority in order to bring that about. But I am sorry I cannot give any definite answer as to whether the Argentine did ask to be admitted, or as to whether it has asked since.

Under the agreement, every nation participating undertakes to maintain a high standard of living internally. That is one point of which I am very strongly in favour. How do we interpret that in Canada? Under the government's policy we are to try to maintain a high degree of employment, but I think we also realize that there are bound to be in this countiy a number of people unemployed, people who will not be covered by unemployment insurance. Just how does the minister interpret "high standard of living" in regard to such people? Are special measures to be adopted to ensure that every individual in Canada is able to obtain sufficient food to give him a decent standard of living? Is it the intention, for instance, to adopt such a procedure as the United States adopted under the food stamp plan? Is some measure of that kind contemplated?

I did not refer to some remarks which were made this afternoon with regard to the United States plan, and the other evening when we were discussing another matter I did not do so, because I hesitate at this moment to discuss United States plans as compared with our own. But I should like to point out, in view of the fact that the question is definitely raised, that under the United States plan as now operating, the parity price plan we discussed the other evening, upon part of which the resolution was based, ninety per cent of parity is provided for only on condition that certain provisions made for the limiting of production are agreed to and carried into effect by the persons who are involved, which means that there is a definite plan made for limiting
production, in spite of what was said this afternoon to the effect that that idea has been dropped.
In Australia, on the other hand-and again I am speaking from memory and I would not want to give the exact figures-the price provided for wheat, for example, is something over seventy cents a bushel at the delivery point on the first 3,000 bushels, but if more than 3,000 bushels are delivered it is just something over fifty cents, I think fifty-three or fifty-four cents.
In other words, in quite a number of nations definite provisions are made that the prices established are established only on limited amounts, and there is no provision for the inducement of unlimited production. I think this country is one of the few exceptions to that. I think, in spite of what has been said, it is the only real exception among the nations which produce surpluses. We have never placed a restriction upon the amount of our product which can be sold. We have on occasion attempted to persuade our people by giving them acreage payments to shift from the production of one food product to another; but we have always said, in any regulations we have made with regard to the delivery of quotas-five bushels per acre for this month and ten for the next, and so on- those are there because of either a shortage of storage space or a lack of markets for the time being for the product. But we have never placed any limitation upon the price which is to be obtained for the product, provided that more of it is produced in a particular year than we have suggested it might be wise to produce. So, the other day, after it had been definitely said in this house last session that farmers would be permitted to deliver only fourteen bushels to the acre, when it was discovered that a market could be found or storage could be found somewhere in Canada for all the wheat they could deliver, that restriction was removed, and farmers who grow thirty or forty bushels to the acre can deliver it all this year.
That is the policy we have been following. It is the policy, I submit, which we said last session1-and1 I hope we shall be able to carry it out-we intended to continue. For example, I do not feel that we would be dealing justly with people, whether farmers or others, Lf we had said to them, during the three or four year period we have just come through, yes, you have had big crops; you have had fine crops or you have had a big production1, and we limited the amount that you could obtain for each unit of your production; but now that the war is over, if you have big production we are only going to take a fraction of it at a price similar to the price you got

United Nations Food Agreement
before. The interpretation we placed upon our obligations in the last session was to the effect that the production during that period, as well as the price, must be still taken into consideration in the period after the war in establishing a reasonable return.
Our method of dealing with this situation has been this. Take butter as an illustration. The ceiling price of butter is thirty-five cents. Farmers in Canada cannot produce butter at thirty-five cents. We have been paying the farmer a subsidy on butter of from eight to ten cents a pound butterfat. It is all very well to say that this is a subsidy to the farmer, but the real consideration that was given was that consumers, under the present wage scales, and with the returns which they were obtaining during the last three years of the war, could not afford to pay more than thirty-five cents a pound for their butter. Therefore, we said, the price is to be thirty-five cents. I am speaking now on the basis of wholesale price at Montreal. Then we took the money out of the treasury to make possible the sale of the product at thirty-five cents. As a result of that, we in Canada are eating forty million pounds more butter a year than we were eating before the war; and we have had to ration butter, not because we are short of butter as compared with the period before the war, but in order to say to the fellow who used to put butter on his potatoes and everything else he was eating and thought he could afford to do so, you will have to forgo some of these luxuries in order to let every child in this country get a proportion of the butter. That is the principle on which we have been proceeding. I submit it is the principle on which we should proceed during this period in order to see to it that our own people are properly fed with the products we produce in this country.

I appreciate the minister's reply, but he did not answer the question I asked. Under this agreement we pledge ourselves to give the people of Canada a high standard of living. I am quite in accord with the minister that we can provide a high standard of living, that we can produce enough food for that, but this is what I am interested in. Do we merely mean a high standard on an average, or are we going to guarantee that every person in Canada has a high standard of living, at least in so far as food is concerned? If that is the intention, then what does the government plan to do in regard to people in this country who may be unemployed, who do not come under unemployment insurance, who have no purchasing power and therefore are not in a position to buy the food that is in abundance in this country ? I asked the minister whether it

was the intention, for instance, to adopt the United States food stamp plan they had before the war. What I want to know is whether this guarantee means we are going to maintain a high standard of living merely based upon the average, or whether that high standard of living is to be given to every individual in this country.
The only reason I did not definitely answer the question with regard to the stamp programme is that I do not want to condemn anything the Americans are doing.
Or any other plan.

I believe the plan I have just outlined will better meet our conditions than any stamp plan they have had in the United States; but the stamp plan may meet their conditions better than anything we have had here. I am not discussing United States conditions; I am discussing Canadian conditions. I think under Canadian conditions we have fed our people;-and when I say "we" I mean all the people of Canada-just as well as those of any nation on the allied side during this war period, and I believe we shall be able to continue to do so in future.

I imagine the hon. member for Acadia was not thinking particularly of the war period but rather of the near and actual starvation which existed in this country before the war and which may exist again after the war, and what the commitments were in that regard.
I presume, Mr. Chairman, that we shall be going through this schedule clause by clause when we come to the preamble, where it is mentioned, because I think we should understand what we are doing. We are making some definite commitments both in regard to our own country and in regard to other nations, and I think we should realize that these must be more than words. Under the united nations charter adopted at San Francisco not only nutrition but full employment is pledged by every nation signing that charter.
What I really rose to ask was this, following the question raised by the hon. member for Lake Centre. Under article XIII of the agreement this is provided:
The organization shall, in accordance with the procedure provided for in the following paragraph, constitute a part of any general international organization to which may be entrusted the coordination of the actiivties of international organizations with specialized responsibiilties.
2. Arrangements for defining the relations between the organization and any such general organization shall be subject to the approval of the conference. Notwithstanding the provision of article XX . . .

Then, it goes on to deal with the matter of amendment. What I was wondering was this. I take it that the general international organization is the united nations international organization which was established at San Francisco. Under that charter we have set up the social and economic council, and that social and economic council provides that certain specialized bodies shall be set up, of which it is anticipated this will be one. At San Francisco, Argentina was admitted as a signatory to the charter. I must say I did not approve that, and I am sorry Canada cast her vote in favour of it, but I am not going into that matter now. However, Argentina was admitted by the conference as a member nation. She accepts the charter drawn up. The charter includes a provision for the establishment of a social and economic council, of which there are to be specialized agencies. If one of the specialized agencies is this food and agriculture council, would it not follow that Argentina would be brought into this organization through membership in the social and economic council and in the united nations organization itself? That is what I was going to ask. Can the minister tell us whether that is so, whether that would follow?

When I was answering the other question it occurred to me that this might be involved in the decision made at San Francisco, but I would not like to undertake to answer that question. The Minister of Justice was at San Francisco; I dio not know whether he would care to answer it. I would not like to undertake to say that Argentina would come in automatically because of anything done at San Francisco. From reading these articles I would- judge that she would have to obtain admission through a two-thirds vote of those already in.

That is the way it appears; yet if there is a specialized agency within the social and economic council, which is one of the chapters of the charter, and the nations agreed to the whole charter, can a nation exclude itself from one of the specialized agencies? That is the point I had in mind.
I do not feel competent to answer that.

I cannot answer the question myself, and I do not know whether the Minister of Justice would care to do so.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I would not attempt to answer the question, but it would appear to me that this organization is being set up 47696-62
United Nations Food Agreement
now in accordance with the terms of this constitution; and the united nations charter has not yet come into operation. When it does come into operation it will be dealing with the food and agriculture organization as an entity existing under its own constitution, and then some modifications may have to be made in order to adopt- the food- and agriculture organization as the specialized agency provided for under the united nations charter. I think, though, that for the time being this organization will come into existence if twenty nations file their acceptance; and from the time twenty nations will have filed their acceptance it will be an autonomous body. Then, because its members also will be members of the united nations, if it becomes the specialized agency there may have to be some modification in the constitution.

As a matter of fact, that is provided for in the constitution itself.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes; but when it does in fact become integrated in the special agencies under the united nations, some modification may -have to be made as a result of the terms of the charter adopted at San Francisco.

We are now dealing with section 2, which -is the operative section; and the gravamen of my remarks this afternoon was directed to the power there given to the governor in council to-
. . . make such appointments, establish such offices, make such orders in council and do such things as appear to him to be necessary for carrying out the provisions of the constitution set out in the schedule to this act or any recommendations of the conference of the food and agriculture organization of the united nations, or of its committees, made pursuant to such provisions.
I am not going to repeat the arguments advanced this afternoon. In this section as it now stands there is in effect an abdication by parliament of the right to deal with any decisions or recommendations made by the conference and the food and agriculture organization When it is set up. The point I was making this afternoon was that matters concerned with the future of agriculture and agricultural and economic relationships for a period of five years should -be submitted to parliament. I therefore submit a suggested amendment to section 2. Subsection 2 I think expresses the general feeling of the committee. Subsection 1 is the operative section, and, indeed, is the only section in the whole bill that affords any opportunity to approve the constitution, although there is



United Nations Food Agreement
no reference therein to that fact. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Eglinton:
That section two, subsection (1) be stricken out and the following substituted therefor:
"2. (1) The constitution of the food and agriculture organization of the united nations as set out in the schedule to this act is hereby approved."
That subsection simply amounts to this, that it affords a direct operative approval by parliament of the constitution of the food and agriculture organization.
When speaking a while ago, the minister said that he desired, and what the government desired was that this house should unanimously approve the constitution. By using direct words to that effect I submit we attain that desire.
Then, so far as subsection 2 of section 2 is concerned, I move that the following be substituted therefor:
The governor in council may do such things as are necessary to carry out the provisions of the said constitution, subject to the approval of parliament within six months thereafter.
In other words, when recommendations are made by the nations comprising the conference of the food and agriculture organization, or by any of its committees, such matters shall be subject to the approval of parliament within six months.
Does that mean that the recommendations could not be acted upon for six months?
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I point out that the hon. member cannot put two amendments to the committee at the same time.

That is correct. I was simply giving the whole picture. I realize full well the truth of what the Chairman has said. However, I wished to give the whole picture at once so that the purpose of my amendments would be before the committee. The first amendment is the one I now move.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I understood that it was one amendment.

Yes.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It is an amendment to strike out subsection 1 of section two, and to substitute the two provisions the hon. member read.

Yes.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I do not think there can be any objection to the first part of that provision. While in my view it may not be

absolutely necessary, once again this should appear to the Canadian people and to the people of the world at large as the action of the Canadian people through its representatives in parliament. As such it should be in such form as to deserve the hearty support of all members of parliament. There may appear to a good many to be some merit in a categorical declaration that the terms of the charter are approved by parliament. The first portion of the amendment would imply that.
Then, as to the second portion, I know the hon. member wishes to have something operative, and wishes Canada to become a member of the organization and to be recognized by the other members of the organization as having done so.
I would fear that the qualifying words: "subject to the approval of parliament within six months thereafter," would make it appear that Canada was accepting in an irrevocable way, because in order to adhere to the charter, instruments of acceptance have to be filed by the government. If that filing of the instrument of acceptance by the government was subject to approval within six months it might be regarded that in the meantime it was not an irrevocable acceptance.
I do not think the hon. member would wish any doubt to become possible as to the validity of the action taken by the government of Canada to make Canada a party of the organization. Moreover the terms used by the hon. member would, I suggest, be too restrictive. Under the charter, all that is necessary at a conference would be one member. Only one representative of a member can vote at the conference, and all that would be necessary to carry out the terms of the constitution would be to have one person there representing Canada.
It is intended, and I think this would be in accordance with the desire of all hon. members, that the delegate be accompanied by proper advisers. That is not necessary under the terms of the constitution, but I think the powers of the governor in council should be such as to do things mentioned in the preamble, such things as are expedient or proper to carry out the purposes of the constitution.
I would fear that with the language suggested by the hon. member it would have to be determined that the thing which was covered by an order in council was necessary, before it could be recognized as valid. I do not think the hon. member would wish to go that far. I suggest it is preferable that recommendations from the conference or from the committees require to be approved by parliament before being acted upon. That would be so under

United Nations Food Agreement
the bill as drafted, in respect of everything requiring the expenditure of money. Before any money could be used to implement a recommendation, it would have to be appropriated by parliament.
But one can conceive that there might be recommendations which would not imply the expenditure of public money. If it were felt that such recommendations should be implemented by this country, they might have to be implemented by provincial legislatures, or they might be such as could be implemented by the dominion parliament. I think in any event they should be subject to the action of the proper legislative body, before being acted upon.
I do not think there would intervene any such delay as would be prejudicial to the effective operation of the organization; for after all, according to its constitution this is not an organization to collect and distribute food. It is an organization to gather statistical information and to make recommendations for the more efficient production and distribution of food. But it is not the instrument that would do the work. When such recommendations are made, if they imply imposing obligations upon Canadian citizens, then it is my personal view that it would be quite proper that they should have to go before the body competent to legislate, whether it be a provincial legislature or this parliament. Certainly we can anticipate that there would be recommendations requiring the action of provincial legislatures.
Mr. DIEFENBAKEiR: That is just what the bill as now constituted does not protect.
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	Does not in terms
protect. But this parliament cannot give to the governor in council the right to do things that parliament itself would not have jurisdiction to do. Whatever delegation is made can only be of powers that are within the control of the one who makes the delegation. On that point I do not think there should be any quarrel between one group and another in this committee. I think we are all concerned with having this food and agriculture organization work to the best possible advantage for mankind generally and it probably would be sufficient to avoid any inconvenience that might result from delay to have the governor in council empowered to do the things proper or expedient to carry out the terms of the constitution. That may involve doing more than the language submitted by the hon. member would cover.
He uses the words "such things as are necessary," but once again all that is necessary for the conference would be the attendance 47696-62J
of one member for Canada. That certainly would not be taking Canada's proper place in the conference. The delegate authorized to vote for Canada at any international conference should have with him quite a large group of technical advisers. What we are contemplating is a delegation that might amount to as many as thirty advisers to the official delegate. I think the language used in the statute should be broad enough to allow the things that are appropriate and expedient to carry out the terms and purposes of the constitution to be done.
I submit to the hon. member that if the language used in the bill were retained and cut off after the words "schedule to this act" in line 24, which would delete the words "or any recommendations of the conference of the food and agriculture organization of the united nations, or of its committees, made pursuant to such provision," taking the first part of his amendment as subsection 1 and having the language down to the words "schedule of the act" as subsection 2, and then numbering the present subsection 2 as subsection 3, we would have something that would correspond with what appears to be the unanimous desire of this committee; that is, that the governor in council do not go beyond performing the things which are proper and expedient to give effect to the constitution and that if there are any recommendations which have to be implemented, requiring the authority of law, whether it be provincial or federal, they go to the legislative body which by the constitution has the right to make law in that regard.

I think the minister has agreed with the contention I raised, that, as this section stood it conveyed too great power to the governor in council. He suggests-that that portion of section 2, subsection lr which would empower the governor in council by order in council to carry out "any recommendations of the conference of the food and agriculture organization of the united nations, or of its committees, made pursuant to such provisions," be deleted. I think the section with the deletion of the portion referred to by the minister would be satisfactory. As it was originally drafted, it conveyed powers far and beyond any ever conveyed to a governor in council at any time. In view of the statement the minister has made I am agreeable to the amendment he suggests, provided that a later section-I take it this will be done, according to the Minister of Agriculture-it is provided that any orders in council made pursuant to section 2, subsection 1. if amended in the manner suggested by the Minister of Justice, will be tabled and made available to parliament.
