Mr. ST. LAURENT: If I understand the hon. member correctly, he still wishes the first part of his amendment retained.

I understood the minister accepted it.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: There can be no objection to that. It is a positive declaration by the house, and there may be many who would find merit in having that expressly declared in the bill. That would be subsection 1 of section 2. What is here, down t-o the words "schedule to this act" would be subsection 2 of section 2 and the present subsection 2 would become subsection 3 of section 2.
That is right.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The amendment moved by the hon. member for Lake Centre is before the committee, but he has intimated that he will accept the amendment suggested by the Minister of Justice. Is the hon. member for Lake Centre withdrawing his amendment?
Yes. We are getting together and accommodating ourselves to the suggestions.
One of you move it and the other second it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is moved by the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent), seconded by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker):
That section 2 (1) be stricken out and the following substituted therefor:
"2. (1) The constitution of the food and agriculture organization of the united nations as set out in thq schedule to this act is hereby approved.
2. (2) The governor in council may make such appointments, establish such offices, make such orders in council and do such things as appear to him to be necessary for carrying out the provisions of the constitution set out in the schedule of this act." And that subsection 2 be renumbered as subsection 3.

Now that the lawyers have agreed as to how this section should appear, I, as a layman, would like to ask a question because it does not seem to cover one of the criticisms I have. Let me read section 2, subsection 2, as now proposed by the Minister of Justice and the hon. member for Lake Centre. It reads:
The governor in council may make such appointments, establish such offices, make such orders in council and do such things as appear to him to be necessary

But it does not stop there. It says:
-as appears to him to be necessary for carrying out the provisions of the constitution.
One of the provisions of the constitution is that this food and agriculture organization

may determine its own budget and may determine the portion of that budget that Canada will pay, and we have only one man on that organization. One of the reasons why I criticized this set-up was that by this bill we are approving the constitution. The constitution allows that organization to determine its own budget and to determine the portion Canada will pay. Then we are asked to give power to the governor in>
council to do all such things as appear to him to be necessary for carrying out the provisions of the constitution.
I ask this question of the Minister of Justice:	Are we not committing ourselves
now to further expenses than the 5-06 per cent of the present suggested budget in case the organization should ask for more? Does the minister get my point?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	The leader of the
opposition has not overlooked the next subsection, which reads:
All expenditures incurred in carrying out the provisions of subsection 1-
That will now be subsection 2:
-of this section shall be defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament.
There is a requirement, in order to have the money available to the extent contemplated by the constitution, that it be appropriated by parliament, and if the hon. gentleman will look at article XVIII, which is the article under which the members undertake to contribute, he will see that it provides:
Each member nation undertakes, subject to the requirements of its constitutional procedure, to contribute to the organization promptly its share of the expenses so determined.

That is the very point,
as determined by these people, and they may raise the proportion we are now required to pay. Under this arrangement we are subscribing to that, and it is only after that, that we are requested to provide additional money.
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	The constitution is
before us. It requires us to accept it as it is and provides that the government undertakes, subject to the requirements of its constitutional procedure, to pay its share of the expenses, and in the authorization that is being given to file an instrument of acceptance there is this subsection 3 which provides that no expenditure by Canada can be made unless parliament appropriates the money. We place . ourselves in a position where by filing the instrument of acceptance, whatever we may do here, we engage the honour of the Canadian nation to comply with the provisions of the constitution. It does not matter what we put into our statute. By filing the instrument of acceptance, that is what we undertake. We

United, Nations Food Agreement
undertake it, or the government of Canada undertakes it, subject to the requirements of its constitutional procedure, and one of the requirements of its constitutional procedure is that the government cannot dispose of money that has not been voted by parliament.

But we have assumed
a debt of honour, and I think any parliament will agree to pay.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I would hope so.

The only recourse that we have, it seems to me, is under article XIX, which provides that if we are dissatisfied with the amount required from Canada, then four years from now, having had the experience, we may give notice of withdrawal from the organization at the end of the five years.
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	There is this moral
recourse as well. There is the implied declaration that the present budget is to be $2,500,000, and that it may go to $5,000,000, and if it were carried beyond that by action of which we disapproved we would have valid grounds for wishing to withdraw. But whatever we put into the legislation being considered by the committee at the present time, if it amounts to authority to the government of Canada to file an instrument of acceptance, we have to take the constitution as written and we assume on behalf of Canada a debt of honour to have parliament appropriate enough money to carry out the obligations implied.

In other words, this
has been agreed to by the nations and we cannot amend the constitution. We must either accept or reject it. That is the position.
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	Yes, and if we file
an instrument of acceptance we accept it and undertake to have parliament appropriate the money required to implement that obligation.

I agree with what
has been said as to complying with the constitution, but we may have gone too far with the amendment. By what clause in this bill have we power to implement recommendations that may come from the committees?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	The governor in
council would not have the power to implement the recommendations, and I do not think it is the feeling of the committee that the governor in council should have that power. I think it is the feeling of the committees that when the recommendations come they should be like the recommendation, for
example, of the international labour organization. They should require legislative action by the proper legislative body and that is what the amendment provides. I do not think the amendment cuts that down at all. It merely says that it will take the recommendations; then the legislative body competent to deal with them will consider them and, if they are thought to be proper, will enact the required legislation.

I do not wish to labour
this point any farther. Nobody has raised any question about approving the constitution. There has been no question of that.. The only question is what the constitution does or what it means and what this organization may do under it. I think the Minister of Justice will agree that that body can determine the size of its own budget, can determine the percentage we pay, and may raise it, and the governor in council has power to do all such things as are necessary to carry that out. But if the Minister of Justice is satisfied I accept his word. But we are voting blindly to that extent. We may have to do it. But the point I wish to make is that we do not want the government to commit us further than the figures given, $2,500,000 the first year and $5,000,000 later on, with Canada's contribution being at the rate of 5-06 per cent, because if we were committed further, this committee will have been misled.
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	If there was an appropriation bill being suggested there would no doubt be limitations inserted, as was done in the United States, where by joint resolution of the two houses of congress an express limitation was put on their contribution. They said that their obligations could not go beyond one million and a quarter.

There is no limitation
like that here.
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	Our appropriation
is not being made by this legislation. This legislation requires that there be further action by parliament to appropriate the money to be expended.
Can the minister state what the appropriation will be for the coming year?

I think the United States provision itself limits it. It is definitely stated that their proportion is twenty-five per cent,, and that twenty-five per cent cannot exceed a certain figure. That in itself limits the-amount which can be spent by the whole organization.
Labour Conditions
We should not be tied by something they do.
We are tied by it under these provisions.

The leader of the opposition said there was no question whether we would accept the constitution. I am giving notice now that there is a question whether we ought to accept the constitution. We have to find out now whether the advantages we can derive from accepting the constitution are such as to recompense us for the dangers which we are likely to run into by accepting the constitution. I do not believe that the Minister of Agriculture or anyone else in this house to-day has shown us specifically any advantage which we can derive, either directly or indirectly, from accepting the constitution. If he can, I shall certainly be a ready listener. The problem which confronts us is, first of all, how to produce the goods, and second, how to distribute them. We have not been shown how we can produce goods any better or distribute them any better by accepting the constitution.
Progress reported.
